The Envelope on the Kitchen Table

Aunt Bev’s kitchen table wore a yellow oilcloth printed with rows of little coffee pots. I sat there the day after we buried her, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving in 2023. In front of me were a long white envelope with a law office’s name in the corner, Bev’s house key on a ring with a plastic daisy that had lost two petals, and a legal pad I’d brought from home.

The will inside the envelope ran five pages. On the first one, Bev named me her executor.

I read it three times. Each time I reached the end I knew exactly what she wanted, and I had no idea what I was supposed to do the following Monday.

So I made a list. I kept the books for my husband Dale’s heating-and-cooling business for 27 years, and a list is what I reach for when I’m frightened and don’t care to say so. In about an hour I had nineteen items. Item two was “Call the bank.” Item four was “Sewing machine to the lady from quilting circle,” because she’d asked about it after the service and I wanted to be kind. Item eleven was “Pay the bills.”

That list was not a good start. Roughly a third of it was in the wrong order, and two items weren’t mine to do yet. The will didn’t mention the sewing machine at all, which meant it belonged with everything else in the estate, and it was not mine to give away that week or for many months after.

What Bev’s will didn’t tell me, because no will does, was the order.

Collect, pay, hand over

An executor is the person a court trusts to collect what someone owned, pay what they owed, and hand over the rest — in that order.

The order is the job. Most of the expensive mistakes I’ve watched executors make, my own included, come down to one of those three steps done too soon. A bill paid before anyone knew how many bills there were. A recliner handed to a nephew before the debts were counted. An account closed before the court had said who was allowed to close it.

Your court papers may call you a personal representative instead of an executor, and if there’s no will you’ll likely be called an administrator. Same three steps, same order.

One more thing before you go further. Being named in a will doesn’t mean you’ve agreed to anything. If you haven’t decided whether to take this on, start with Chapter 1, which assumes no is a perfectly respectable answer.

Fourteen months

Bev’s estate took fourteen months. By most measures it wasn’t complicated: a widow with no children, one house, a handful of accounts, a car and a storage unit. It still took fourteen months, and I worked on it nearly every week.

For a sense of scale from a court that puts it in writing, the California Courts Self-Help Guide says a formal probate case there “typically takes 9 to 18 months and can sometimes take even longer.” That’s one state’s estimate, and I’m in Ohio. Yours may run faster or slower. Some estates qualify for a shorter small-estate process and never see a full court case at all, which Chapter 2 helps you check. Others stretch out because a house won’t sell or an heir won’t sign.

Most of that time is waiting. The work comes in bursts: a heavy stretch at the start, hard weeks around the inventory and the bills, a knot of tax forms, then a scramble at the end. In between, you wait for windows to close, and the waiting is part of what protects you.

People will tell you there’s no hurry. That’s half right, and the wrong half costs money. There’s no hurry to pay ordinary bills or to hand anything out. There are tax deadlines, though, and the estate tax return’s clock starts on the date of death without sending you a reminder. Chapters 8 and 9 put those dates on your calendar.

Who this is for, and what it hands off

This book is for the person whose name is in the will, or who is about to ask a court to appoint them. You probably have a job. You may have siblings with opinions. You almost certainly have a stack of mail addressed to someone who can’t open it.

It’s written for readers in all fifty states, so it can’t be the last word on any one of them. Probate is state law. Deadlines, forms, fees and even the names of things change at the state line, and sometimes at the county line. When I use California as the worked example, it’s because California’s court website lays out every stage in plain language, not because your state follows it. At the end of each stage I’ll send you to two places to confirm what you’ve read: your state court’s self-help website, and the probate clerk in the county where the person lived. A clerk can’t give you legal advice. A clerk can tell you which form, which deadline, and what the local judge expects to see on it.

Two subjects belong to the other books in this series. The first two weeks after a death — arrangements, death certificates, telling Social Security and everyone else — are covered in The First 90 Days After a Parent Dies. Writing your own will is Estate Planning for Beginners. This book picks up once the service is over and the paperwork is legally yours to carry.

Where I’ll tell you to stop

I have never held a law license or a tax credential of any kind. I’m a bookkeeper who settled three estates in one county over eight years — my father’s, my mother’s, then Bev’s — and learned most of it by getting something wrong once. My stories come from those three. The rules come from places you can check yourself: the IRS, the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and state court self-help sites. Every number carries its year and the agency that published it, because figures change, and a number without a date is a rumor.

Some moments in this job call for a careful amateur to put the pen down and phone a lawyer. When we reach one, I’ll say so in that paragraph rather than in small print at the back, and I’ll tell you why. A will someone is challenging. More debt than money. A business or farm ground. An estate anywhere near the federal estate tax line, or a surviving husband or wife. A beneficiary who has stopped returning your calls and started mentioning a lawyer of their own.

Sam, the Chillicothe estate lawyer who handled Bev’s case, taught me that a lawyer’s time is best spent on a short list of good questions. You’ll meet him again. Hiring help isn’t a confession that you can’t do the job, and Chapter 1 covers who pays for it.

How to read it

Read Chapters 1 through 3 this week, in order. They’re the decisions: whether to serve, what you actually control, and how the court appoints you.

The rest is machinery and money. Getting your authority recognized, the estate’s tax number and bank account, the inventory, the bills, two kinds of tax return, handing things out, closing the file and getting paid, with the family running underneath all of it. Those chapters aren’t meant for one weekend. Keep them beside the folder and open each one when you get there.

Every chapter has one tool — a worksheet, a checklist, a decision rule or a script. Use them on paper. You’ll want to show your work later, possibly to a judge.

The folder

Before Chapter 1, start a folder. That first evening, Dale brought a one-inch white binder in from his office and set it next to my legal pad.

“You’ll want tabs,” he said.

He was right. Whatever you use, a binder, a file box or a fat envelope with a rubber band around it, this book calls it the folder, and later chapters will add to it. On day one it holds four things.

  1. A copy of the will. Photocopy it and keep the original somewhere safe, flat and unmarked. Don’t write on it. Chapter 3 covers where your state wants the original and how soon.
  2. The court’s contact page. The name of the probate court in the county where the person lived, the clerk’s phone number, office hours and street address, and the web address of your state court’s self-help pages.
  3. A phone log. Every call, every visit: the date, who you spoke to, what they told you, and what they asked you to send. Chapter 4 adds columns. Mine for Bev filled several pages.
  4. A money notebook. Every dollar you spend out of your own pocket on the estate, with the date, who you paid, what it was for and the receipt stapled behind the page. Chapter 5 shows how to repay yourself properly.

Here’s one line from my phone log, written the Monday after Thanksgiving:

Mon., Nov. 27, 2023, 9:10 a.m. Called Sam’s office. Spoke to the woman at the front desk. First appointment Thursday at 10. Bring the original will, Bev’s house key and a list of what she owned, best guess.

And the first entry in the money notebook, from that same afternoon:

Nov. 27, 2023. Copy counter at the office-supply store on Bridge Street. Four copies of Bev’s will, five pages each. $3.00, my own debit card. Receipt stapled behind.

Neither one is interesting, which is the point. Nobody writes an exciting phone log.

The log line holds three things memory drops first: when you did something, who told you what, and what they asked you to bring. Months later, when a relative asks why nothing happened until December, or an office insists you never called, you turn to the page and read it out.

The money line ties a dollar amount to a date, a reason and a piece of paper. At the end of the case someone will add up everything that came into the estate and everything that went out, and every dollar you fronted has to appear in that count, with proof, or you’ve paid it yourself. Three dollars doesn’t matter. Three dollars plus every stamp, every certified copy and every tank of gas across fourteen months adds up to real money, and only the notebook knows the total.

The log and the notebook are my habits, not legal requirements. The reason behind them is real, though. In California, the court expects a final account of the estate’s money at the end of the case unless everyone entitled to a share signs a written waiver, and other states have their own versions of that reckoning. Fourteen months is a long time to reconstruct from memory.

Tonight, write today’s date on the first line of the phone log, even if you haven’t called anyone yet.

Start the log.

Chapter 1: You Can Say No

Sam’s office was on the second floor above an insurance agency, up a flight of stairs with a brass rail somebody kept polished. I was there at ten o’clock on Thursday, November 30, the appointment from my phone log, with Bev’s original will in a manila folder on my lap.

Sam read all five pages without a word. Then he took off his glasses, set them on the desk blotter and asked, “Do you want to do this?”

“She named me,” I said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He let it sit long enough that I heard the radiator tick under the window. I said yes before he’d put his glasses back on.

I’d still say yes. But I’d have said it a week later, and by the end of this chapter you’ll see why.

Named is not the same as agreed

A will nominates. It doesn’t conscript. The person who wrote it can choose you, and nobody, a judge included, can make you take the job. Bev’s will was her request. My yes was a separate act, and so is yours.

Until a court has put you in charge, you can turn the job down. While you decide, don’t distribute, sell or dispose of anything that belonged to the person who died. California’s court self-help guide, as it read in October 2026, says a judge appoints the personal representative at a hearing, and that a representative must be appointed to get access to the person’s bank records. Other states handle the weeks before appointment in their own ways. If a bill or an action seems necessary to preserve property in the meantime, ask the probate clerk what the court’s current procedure, forms and deadlines are for an urgent request. For authority, liability, or a disputed legal reading, ask the estate’s lawyer, including whether anyone may pay that bill before a court has appointed anyone. Write down the answer and keep the receipt for anything you pay.

Look first for an alternate, a second name in the will, sometimes a third, who serves if the first person can’t or won’t. A careful will names one.

If there’s no alternate, or the alternate says no too, the court chooses, and state law tells it whom to prefer. California’s court self-help guide lays out that state’s order plainly, as it read in 2026: a surviving spouse or domestic partner first, then a child, a grandchild, a parent and a sibling, with a judge deciding who actually has priority. Your state has its own list. The probate clerk can tell you where to find it.

Once you’re appointed, the picture changes. You’d be asking the same court to let you step down, under your state’s rules, and that’s a conversation for a lawyer rather than a form you pick up at the counter. The time to decide is now, before anything gets filed with your name on it as the person in charge.

Decide first.

What the job actually takes

People who haven’t done it picture a few signatures. Here is the bill as I’d itemize it.

Time comes first. You already have California’s estimate and my fourteen months, so here’s the texture instead. The job lives inside your week. A call on your lunch break. A form at the kitchen table after supper. A Saturday morning sorting statements into piles on the dining room floor. Some weeks it’s twenty minutes. A few weeks early on, it ate most of my evenings, and Dale learned to make his own supper without being asked.

Then there’s money, which surprises nearly everyone. The estate is generally expected to pay the costs of settling itself, eventually. At the start, though, its money is usually sitting in accounts nobody can touch yet, so the person doing the work pays. California’s self-help guide says the personal representative usually pays fees upfront and gets paid back from the estate later. In 2026 that guide puts the typical California filing fee at $435.00 and says the costs of administration are “often well over $1,000.00 and can be much more.” Other states charge other amounts. The clerk will tell you yours over the phone.

For Bev’s case I fronted the filing fee and a string of smaller costs out of Dale’s and my checking account, before the estate had an account of its own. I got every dollar back, because of the money notebook. That’s my story, not a promise. California says these costs are typically repaid, and whether yours are can depend on your state’s rules, whether the expense was necessary, whether you can document it, whether the court approves it and whether the estate has money left to pay it. If I’d been a year from retirement with nothing set aside, that wait would have been a real hardship. It’s a fair thing to weigh before you agree.

The third cost never shows up on a receipt. You’ll spend a year as the person who says “not yet.” Not yet on the furniture. Not yet on the money. Not yet on selling the house your sister thinks should go on the market next week. Some people find that easy. I kept books for a living, and I still found it wearing.

Whether you get paid for any of this has a different answer in different states, and it waits for Chapter 11.

The four duties, in plain words

Once a court appoints you, you’re a fiduciary. The word means you’re handling property that belongs to somebody else, and the law expects more care from you with it than you might take with your own.

There’s no federal handbook written for executors, and I want to say that plainly, because I’ve seen people recommend one that doesn’t exist. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau publishes a free series called Managing Someone Else’s Money. Its page, as last updated in June 2026, offers guides for four roles: agents under a power of attorney, court-appointed guardians and conservators, trustees, and government fiduciaries such as representative payees. There’s no executor guide in the set.

What those guides share is a set of four basic duties. They carry over to an estate well enough that I use them as my own checklist. Your state’s law sets your real duties, and it may ask for more, but you won’t go far wrong starting here.

Act for the people the estate now belongs to, not for yourself. If you’re also a beneficiary, as family executors very often are, you get your share and not a penny of advantage. You don’t pick first. You don’t buy the car from the estate at a family price unless the court or the estate’s lawyer has said you may.

Manage the money carefully. Nothing clever. The estate’s cash doesn’t go into whatever your brother-in-law is excited about this year. It should arrive at the end in about the shape it started, minus honest costs.

Keep it separate. The estate’s money never sits in your account, not overnight, not for convenience. Chapter 5 shows you how to set that up.

Keep records. Every dollar and every decision, written down when it happens, in the folder.

None of the four is hard to understand. Doing them on a Tuesday night, tired, with a cousin on the phone, is another matter.

Five questions that decide it

When someone asks me whether they should serve, I don’t ask whether they’re organized. I ask five other things.

Do you live near the court? Most of the work happens by phone and mail, but not all of it, and the clerk’s window keeps business hours. I stood at that window more than once for Bev. If the person lived three states away from you, ask the clerk now how much has to be done in person, and whether your state puts any conditions on an executor who lives somewhere else.

Can you be even-handed with your siblings? Not friendly. Even-handed. If your brother borrowed money from Mom and never paid it back, can you treat that as a fact to raise with the lawyer instead of a score to settle?

Is there something in the estate that’s a job by itself? A business that still has customers. Farm ground with a tenant on it. A rental house. A house so full that emptying it is a summer’s work. Any one of these can double the job, and some need a professional in the first week.

Can you say no to people you love? Someone will want something early. A cousin will ask for the good tools out of the garage, meaning well, before anyone has counted what the estate owes. If refusing that cousin would cost you a month of sleep, count it.

Can you spare a year of Saturdays? Not all of them. Enough that you’ll notice.

Saying no, early and on paper

If your answers come out against you, decline, and do it soon. The kindest no is the early one, because every week you spend deciding is a week the alternate can’t start.

Tell the alternate first, privately, so they hear it from you and not from a court notice. Then tell the rest of the family in one message sent to all of them at once, so nobody gets a different version. Keep it short. You’ve thought it through, you won’t be serving, the will names someone else next, and you’ll hand over everything you’ve gathered.

Then make it official. Ask the probate clerk exactly what your court needs from you in writing to put your refusal on record, and get it filed. A phone call to your sister is not a refusal anybody else can rely on.

Whether to serve and what the will leaves you are two separate questions, usually on two separate pages. Read yours anyway, and if any wording seems to tie a gift to serving, ask a lawyer before you decide.

Hand over what you have in one envelope with a list clipped to the front: the copy of the will, your phone log and the money notebook. That last one matters. List every documented estate-related payment so the next representative can request reimbursement under your state’s rules. Nobody can ask to repay a cost that nobody wrote down.

Two names on one line

Some wills name two people to serve together. Usually it’s two siblings, sometimes a sibling and a spouse. It sounds fair, and it often is. It’s also slower.

California’s self-help guide says two or more people can represent an estate together, but they “must always act together.” In practice that means both signatures, both opinions and both calendars on everything, for the whole case. If you and your co-executor think alike and live near each other, that’s a safeguard, because nobody can quietly empty an account. If you don’t, it’s a deadlock with a filing fee.

Other states treat co-executors differently, and some wills spell out how the two should split the work. Before you agree to serve with someone, ask the clerk how your court handles two representatives. Then sit down with the other person and agree, on paper, who calls whom, who keeps the folder and how you’ll settle a disagreement. If you can’t have that conversation calmly now, you’ve learned something useful.

Yes, with conditions

You can say yes and still decide you won’t do it alone. Hiring a lawyer to advise the executor is ordinary, and so is the estate paying for it. California’s guide, for one, says you can usually pay a lawyer’s fees from the property in the estate, and that a representative handling the case without a lawyer can often pay for a consultation on a single question along the way. How your state approves those fees varies. Ask.

People say hiring a lawyer means admitting you can’t handle it. That’s backward. A lawyer is how a careful amateur avoids the handful of mistakes that can leave you personally on the hook for money that was never yours. Sam didn’t settle Bev’s estate for me. He told me what to file and in what order, I did most of the legwork, and his time came out of the estate.

Some situations make professional help the price of my yes. They’re the stop signs I named in the introduction: a fight over the will, more debt than money, a business or farm, an estate near the federal tax line or a surviving spouse, a beneficiary who has started talking about a lawyer. If one of them is already in front of you, book an hour with a probate lawyer before you either accept or decline. That hour commits you to nothing and tells you what you’d be signing up for. Add a CPA to the list if the person ran a business, owned rentals or left years of tax returns unfiled.

Put the condition into your answer. “Yes, if the estate hires a lawyer from the start” is a complete sentence, and a reasonable one.

What I’d change

I said yes three times in eight years, and the first two hardly count as decisions. When my father died in 2016 and my mother in 2019, I was the one who lived twenty minutes from the house, my brother was in Tucson, and the question never came up. The work was there, so I did it.

Bev’s estate was the only time anyone actually asked me. I answered before Sam had his glasses back on.

Dale was at the kitchen table when I got home, reading the paper. I told him the whole morning. He folded the paper in half and said, “Did you ask what it costs to start?”

I hadn’t. I hadn’t asked how much I’d have to put in before the estate could pay me back, or roughly when that would be. I hadn’t driven out to look at the storage unit, which took far more of that year than I’d have guessed. And I hadn’t told Dale our Saturdays were spoken for until after I’d promised them away.

None of it would have changed my answer. Bev had no children of her own, and I knew her well enough to do the job her way. But a week would have let me say yes on terms: a rough figure from Sam for what I’d front and what his help would cost, a look inside that storage unit, and a conversation at home before the promise instead of after it.

Take the week.

One caution with it. If you’re the one holding the original will, call the clerk this week and ask whether your state wants it delivered by a certain date. That clock may not wait for your decision, and Chapter 3 covers it.

The honest yes/no worksheet

Write these nine questions on one sheet of paper. Answer each with one word: yes, with help or no. A “no” means a hard no. Not “I’d rather not,” but “I can’t, I won’t, or it would cost me something I’m not willing to pay.”

  1. Can I get to the probate court in the county where they lived, during business hours, when I’m needed?
  2. Can I give this a few hours most weeks for a year or more, with heavier stretches?
  3. Can I pay some costs out of my own pocket and wait months to be repaid?
  4. Can I treat every beneficiary the same way, including myself and the one I get along with least?
  5. Can I tell a relative no, in writing, and hold to it?
  6. Is the estate free of anything that’s a job on its own: a business, farm ground, rentals, a house that will take a season to empty?
  7. Is everyone likely to accept the will as written?
  8. Does the estate clearly own more than it owes?
  9. Will I keep the folder up, every call and every dollar, from the first week to the last?

Then count your noes.

None: the worksheet found no obvious stop sign. Confirm the role, the costs and your court’s local requirements, then decide. Declining is still allowed. Your “with help” answers are your list of who to hire.

One: serve only if you can turn that one into “with help” before you accept, and name the help — the lawyer, the CPA, the cousin with a truck.

Two or more: decline, or accept only with a probate lawyer engaged from the start, and say that condition out loud when you give your answer.

Questions 6, 7 and 8 weigh more than the rest. A no on any of them is the kind that turns a hard year into a court fight, so take it to a professional whatever your total.

Date the sheet and put it in the folder. If you change your mind in March, you’ll want to know what you were thinking in November.

When I finally answered Sam, he wrote it on his yellow pad with the date underneath, the way he wrote everything down. Fill in the sheet tonight. Sleep on it once. Then give your answer, to the family, the alternate and the clerk, before the week is out.

Chapter 2: What You Control as Executor, and What You Don’t

Marlene came across the road at ten past eight on a Saturday in March 2026, carrying a cinnamon coffee cake in a glass pan under a dish towel and a canvas tote bag over one shoulder. She set both on my counter and took the towel off the cake first. That’s how I knew it was serious.

Her late husband’s older brother, Ed, had died that February in Peoria, Illinois. He was a widower with no children, a rented apartment and a twelve-year-old sedan titled and registered with the Illinois Secretary of State, and in a will he’d signed in 2019 he named Marlene his executor.

The tote bag held what she’d found when she cleared his apartment. A credit union statement. A brokerage statement. A letter from his old employer’s benefits office. The car title. And a printout listing three Peoria probate lawyers, with their hourly rates written beside each name in her handwriting.

“It all has to go through court,” she said. “Doesn’t it?”

I told her I didn’t know yet, and neither did she, and that was the first useful thing either of us had said all morning.

A will reaches less than you think

Most people in Marlene’s chair start from the same picture. The will is the map, so everything the person owned now belongs to the executor to gather up. That picture is wrong in a way that costs money and friendships.

Probate is the court process that recognizes the will if there is one, appoints someone to act for the estate, and handles whatever the person owned that doesn’t pass some other way. California’s court self-help guide adds the line that surprises people: an estate may need to go through probate even if the person had a will. A will isn’t a way around court. It’s the instructions for the part court handles.

Your authority as executor covers that part, and that part is often a good deal smaller than the pile on the counter.

The other ways property passes — a surviving joint owner, a beneficiary named on an account or policy, a trust — are how people plan, and setting them up belongs to Estate Planning for Beginners. You’re past planning. Your job is to find out, item by item, which way each thing is actually going, and to prove it on paper before you act on it.

Get the paper

The protocol has three steps, and you run all three on every item. The house, the car, each account, each policy, the storage unit.

Step one: get the evidence. Not what the family remembers. Not what Mom said at Easter about who gets the savings. The document, with a date on it.

For real estate, that’s the deed as recorded. California’s guide points out that deeds are public records, kept at the county recorder’s office where the property sits, so you can usually request a copy before anyone has appointed you. Your county has an equivalent office, and its website will tell you which one. When I pulled Bev’s deed at the Ross County recorder’s office, it showed her name alone, and that line on my sheet took ten minutes.

For a vehicle, it’s the certificate of title. Read the owner line and look for a second name.

For a bank, credit union or brokerage account, the statement’s titling line is a start. The better evidence is the institution’s written answer to one question: is there a joint owner, a payable-on-death or transfer-on-death beneficiary, or a trust on this account? Getting that answer can take patience. California’s guide says bank records are private and a personal representative must be appointed to get access, though statements found at home often show a good deal. Some institutions may answer a named executor who sends a death certificate and a copy of the will. Others won’t say a word until you hold court papers, which Chapter 3 covers.

For life insurance, annuities and retirement accounts, you want the company’s written statement of the beneficiary on record. Not the copy in the desk drawer from 1998. The company’s file is the one that counts, and the person may have changed it since.

Ask in writing.

Step two: decide whether you have authority over it. These are rules of thumb, not law, and your state may differ at the edges.

If it’s in the person’s name alone, with no surviving co-owner and no living beneficiary named, the answer is usually yes. It’s yours to handle through the estate.

If a living beneficiary is named on it, the answer is usually no. California’s guide notes that people named as beneficiaries on a retirement or bank account may have their own decisions to make and steps to take to claim the property. Those steps are theirs.

If there’s a surviving joint owner with a right of survivorship, usually no. If a trust owns it, usually no. The trustee handles trust property, and the trustee may or may not be you.

Marriage complicates this. California’s guide warns that a surviving spouse or domestic partner may own part of a piece of property even when they aren’t listed as an owner, depending on whether it’s community property or separate property. If the person was married when they died, don’t decide that question yourself.

Step three: mark anything that doesn’t fit cleanly as “unclear,” and send it to a lawyer before you touch it. A deed with two names and no survivorship wording. A beneficiary who died before the person did. A trust you can’t confirm ever held the property. A form your brother says was signed the week Dad stopped recognizing anyone.

You’ll be tempted to settle these by common sense. Don’t. Common sense about titles can be wrong, and an executor who acts on a wrong guess may have to answer for it personally.

What “no” means in practice

When an item comes back “no authority,” it isn’t yours to manage, sell or hand out. You don’t move it, you don’t use it to pay bills, and you don’t call the company to hurry along your sister’s claim unless she asks you to.

Here is the part people argue with. Say your mother’s life insurance names your sister, and the estate is short. The funeral home has sent a final bill, there’s a credit card balance, and the estate account holds less than both. The policy money generally isn’t the estate’s, and as executor you generally have no say over it. Your sister may decide to help. That’s her decision, made with her own money.

Whether a creditor can ever reach property that passed outside the estate is a question of state law, and the answer can differ from one state to the next. That belongs to a lawyer, and it isn’t something you act on yourself.

The same goes for two suspicions families raise in the first month. One is that a beneficiary form was invalid: signed under pressure, signed when the person couldn’t understand it, or never properly filed. The other is that a joint account was only ever meant to help pay the bills and was never meant as a gift. Both are lawyer questions, not self-help ones, and both turn on facts and state law a book can’t weigh for you. If either one is in front of you, mark the line unclear and book the hour.

“No authority” doesn’t mean you forget the item. Keep a separate page in the folder for everything that passed outside the estate, with the evidence beside each line. The inventory you’ll file with the court lists only what the estate controls. The tax side looks wider. The IRS’s estate tax page, last reviewed in December 2025, lists insurance, trusts and annuities among the things that can count toward what a person owned for estate tax purposes, and Chapter 9 sorts out whether that matters for you. For most families it won’t. You want the page anyway.

When the whole case may be avoidable

Some estates never need a full probate case. States commonly offer a shorter procedure for estates that qualify, often a sworn affidavit or a brief court petition, but the conditions and the thresholds differ, so check your state court’s current page and your probate clerk before you assume either way. The limits are frequently higher than people expect.

California is the clearest example of how these numbers work. According to the California courts’ table of summary procedures, personal property can be collected without the full probate process when the estate is worth no more than $208,850, for deaths on or after April 1, 2025. A separate, shorter court petition can transfer the person’s main home in California when it’s worth no more than $750,000; Assembly Bill 2016 raised that limit and narrowed it to the main home. The Judicial Council adjusts these amounts every three years, and the next update is set for April 1, 2028.

Notice that the limit depends on the date of death, not the date you file. California’s personal property figure was $166,250 for deaths before April 2022. It’s been raised twice since.

Illinois shows how differently another state can build the same idea, and how much it asks of the person signing. The Illinois courts’ approved statewide small estate affidavit, in the version dated November 13, 2025, is a three-page sworn form you fill in yourself. Excluding motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State, the person’s entire personal estate passing to anyone by will or by intestacy must not exceed $150,000. You swear that no letters of office are outstanding on the estate and that no petition for letters is contemplated or pending in Illinois or in any other jurisdiction, to your knowledge. If there’s a will, it must have been filed with the clerk of an appropriate court, and a certified copy goes attached to your affidavit. You state you’re unaware of any dispute or potential conflict about the heirship or the will. The form reaches personal property. It does nothing about real estate.

Then comes the part people hope they can skip. Debts don’t vanish because you’re using the short form. The affidavit gives you two choices in paragraph 7: either all the funeral expenses and other debts are already paid, or every known unpaid debt is listed and classified, with the creditor’s name, post office address and amount. Illinois sorts those debts into seven classes, running from funeral and burial expenses and the costs of administration down to a seventh class for all other claims. You then sign paragraph 7.5. It says you understand that valid claims must be paid by you from the estate before any distribution is made to any heir or legatee. If the estate can’t cover one class, the claims in that class are paid pro rata. Paragraph 10.5 has you agree to indemnify creditors, heirs, legatees and any institution that relies on your affidavit for whatever they lose through an act or omission of yours, plus their attorney’s fees.

Read those two paragraphs twice. A contested claim, or any real uncertainty about which class a debt sits in, is an Illinois probate lawyer’s hour, not a kitchen-table decision.

That’s where Marlene’s tote bag ended up.

She sent a short letter to each of the three institutions, with a copy of Ed’s death certificate and his will, asking the one question. The brokerage wrote back that the account was registered transfer-on-death to her two grown children and that it would deal with them directly. The benefits office wrote that the group life policy named Ed’s late wife’s sister. The credit union confirmed that the checking account was in Ed’s name alone, with no joint owner and no beneficiary. That account, his furniture and some cash in a coffee can were well under $150,000. The sedan was registered with the Illinois Secretary of State, so it sat outside that figure. He’d rented, so there was no real estate.

Ed owed money, the way most people do. A final electric bill. A cell phone bill for February. The funeral home. A card balance of a few hundred dollars. Marlene listed every one of them on the affidavit in its class, with the address and the amount, and paid them out of Ed’s checking before a dollar went to anyone named in the will. No one in the family had been to court about Ed, and no one meant to, which is what let her sign paragraph 5 honestly.

She filed Ed’s will with the probate clerk in Peoria, attached a certified copy to the affidavit, and paid a Peoria lawyer for one hour to read the whole thing before she signed it. She never opened a court case. Her letters went out in the first week of April 2026, and the last answer came back three weeks later.

She carried the last letter across the road at the end of April, with no cake this time. “I could have saved myself the cinnamon,” she said.

Your state’s rule, in ten minutes

You don’t need a lawyer to find out whether your state has a small-estate process. You need ten minutes and a skeptical eye.

Search for your state’s name plus “small estate affidavit,” and open the result from your state court’s own website, not a law firm’s blog or a forum thread. Blogs go stale, and these limits move. As you read, write down four answers on the authority check sheet:

  1. What is the current limit, and for deaths on or after what date?
  2. What counts toward the limit? Vehicles, real estate, only personal property?
  3. How does the process handle debts: must they be paid first, listed, or ranked in classes?
  4. Is there a waiting period after the death before the process can be used?
  5. Does the process require filing anything with the court, such as the will or a certified copy of it?

Then phone the clerk’s office in the person’s home county and read your answers back. The clerk can’t advise you on whether to use the process. The clerk can tell you whether the page you read is current, which form the county uses and whether anything local applies.

Write down the date you checked and who confirmed it. If the estate is close to the limit, or any of the conditions is shaky, or you can’t say with a straight face that you know what the person owed, that’s an hour with a lawyer, not a judgment call at the kitchen table. A small-estate affidavit is a sworn document, often with your own indemnity attached, and you want to be sure every statement in it is true before your name goes at the bottom.

Open, administer, close

If the estate is too large for the short process, or the conditions don’t fit, you’re headed for a full case. California’s guide describes a formal probate case in three parts: opening the case, administering the estate, and closing it. Your state will use its own names and forms, but the shape is a useful map, and it’s how the rest of this book runs.

Chapter 3 is the opening: getting the court to appoint you. Chapters 4 through 9 are the administering, and Chapters 10 and 11 are the closing.

Before you go on, hold this chapter up against your own state’s court pages and the county clerk’s office that handles probate where the person lived. Procedure, blank forms and filing dates are the clerk’s ground, and the clerk beats me on all three. Your powers, your exposure and any rule two people read two ways: that’s lawyer territory.

The authority check

One sheet of paper, or as many as it takes, one line per item. Every line has five parts:

  1. Item. What it is and where it’s held, with only the last four digits of any account number.
  2. Evidence. The document you’re relying on and its date: recorded deed, title, the institution’s letter, the insurer’s beneficiary statement.
  3. Authority. Yes, no or unclear. Nothing else.
  4. Confirmed by. Who told you, and when. A name at the institution, the clerk, the lawyer.
  5. Sent to counsel. For every unclear line, the date you sent it and the date the answer came back.

Here are three lines the way I’d write them. The first is from Bev’s estate. The other two are invented examples of the kinds of lines you’ll see.

House, Bev’s address. Recorded deed, copy from the Ross County recorder. Authority: yes. Confirmed by: the deed itself, plus Sam.

Brokerage account ending 4417. Firm’s letter dated April 9: transfer-on-death to two named beneficiaries. Authority: no. Confirmed by: the firm’s estate services department. Copy on the outside-the-estate page.

Savings ending 0932. Statement shows a nephew as joint owner, added 2021; nephew says it was “just to help with bills.” Authority: unclear. Sent to counsel May 2.

Then the decision rule, which I’d hold to whatever your state:

  • Nothing marked unclear gets touched until a lawyer has answered in writing.
  • Nothing marked no goes into the estate’s account or onto the court inventory. It goes on the separate page.
  • Nothing marked yes moves until you have authority to move it, either the court’s appointment or a small-estate process your clerk has confirmed you qualify for.

Write today’s date at the top and file it behind the yes/no worksheet from Chapter 1. You’ll come back to it more than you expect. When Chapter 6 asks what goes on the inventory, the yes lines are your starting list. When a cousin asks why the insurance money didn’t pay the hospital, the no lines are your answer, with the paper behind them.

Start with the item you’re surest of. Then do the one you’re least sure of, while you still have the energy to chase it.

Chapter 3: Getting the Court to Say You’re the Executor

The deputy clerk at the Ross County Probate Court slid four envelopes under the glass on the second Tuesday of January 2024. Each held one certified copy of my Letters of Authority for Bev’s estate, with the court’s raised seal pressed into the corner. I counted them twice, put them in my handbag and felt, for about a week, extremely well organized.

I’d counted four places that would want proof. The bank downtown. The second bank, out by the bypass. The Bureau of Motor Vehicles, for Bev’s car. The title company, whenever the house sold.

I needed six.

The company insuring Bev’s empty house wanted one before it would put the estate’s name on the policy. And there was an annuity I didn’t know existed yet, which Chapter 6 gets to. Both kept their copies. In March I was back at the same window, ordering two more, and the deputy clerk remembered me.

Dale was at the sink rinsing out his thermos when I came in that afternoon. “Next time,” he said, “count the ones you haven’t found yet.”

The court’s paper is what opens doors. The will doesn’t.

The original will has a clock

Start with the will, because the will may have a deadline before you’ve decided anything else.

California’s court self-help guide says it without decoration: if you find an original will, you must deliver it to the court. California Probate Code section 8200, as published for 2026, adds the clock. Unless a petition for probate gets filed first, whoever has the original must deliver it within 30 days of learning about the death to the clerk of the superior court in the county where the estate may be administered, in person or by registered or certified mail. That person also has to send a copy to the executor named in the will. And a custodian who fails to do it can be liable for the damages anyone suffers because of it.

Thirty days is California’s number. It isn’t a national one, and I won’t give you a national one, because there isn’t one I can point you to. Your state has its own statute and may have its own clock. Look it up this week, on your state court’s self-help site or by phoning the probate clerk, and write the deadline on the front of the folder.

For Bev’s will, this was the easy part. The original was in the law office’s envelope I’d opened at her kitchen table, and on November 30 I carried it up the stairs to Sam’s office in a manila folder. Sam’s office handled the filing. I kept the photocopies in the folder, and I didn’t write on the original, then or ever.

Two situations change this, and both belong to a lawyer from the first phone call.

The first is when you can find only a copy. A photocopy, a scan someone emailed, a carbon from a drawer. Whether a court will accept anything less than the original is a legal question with a lot riding on it, and you don’t want to guess.

The second is when someone else has the original and won’t hand it over. That’s not a family disagreement you settle at Sunday dinner. It’s a lawyer letter.

Which court, and which county

Probate is handled county by county, so the first practical question is which courthouse.

The general answer is the county where the person lived when they died. California’s guide says the case is filed in the county where the person lived, and that if they lived outside California but owned property there, the case goes in the California county where that property sits.

That second rule hints at something bigger. If the person owned a house or land in a second state, that property may need its own proceeding there, under that state’s law. Out-of-state real estate is a lawyer question before it’s anything else. Don’t assume the court back home can reach a cabin three states away.

Once you know the county, find its probate court’s website and the clerk’s phone number, if they aren’t already on the court’s contact page in your folder. Call before you go. Ask what the court’s hours are for filing, whether it takes filings by mail or online, and whether it has a self-help center or a list of local rules for probate. Some counties have their own forms and their own preferences on top of the state’s.

Call first.

The petition that opens the case

Every formal case starts with a request asking the court to open it and appoint someone. In California that’s the Petition for Probate, form DE-111, which the courts describe as asking the court to start the process for distributing a deceased person’s property, paying their debts and settling their financial affairs. The person who files it is called the petitioner. Usually that’s you.

Other states have their own petition or application, with its own name and number. The clerk can tell you which one your court uses. Some states post the form on the state court site; some counties hand it out at the window.

The petition doesn’t travel alone. California’s guide says you file it “along with other court forms,” and one of them is worth reading slowly before you sign anything. Form DE-147, Duties and Liabilities of Personal Representative, explains a representative’s duties and what can happen if they aren’t carried out, and people asking to be appointed use it to tell the court they’ve received it. Read every line. It’s the job description, written by the people who’ll be checking your work.

Then the money. You’ll pay the filing fee from Chapter 1, California’s typical $435.00, unless you apply for a fee waiver, which California allows if you can show financial hardship. California’s court site lists certified copies of court papers among the fees a granted waiver can cover, which matters more than it sounds once you start counting Letters. Either way, these fees can usually be paid or reimbursed from the estate later. Write the check, staple the receipt into the money notebook, and move on.

When you file, the California clerk stamps the forms and gives you a hearing date and a department number. That date is the next fixed point in your life for a while. Put it on the calendar in ink.

My own appointment for Bev was quieter than the California version you’re reading about. Sam’s office prepared the papers, I signed at his desk where the tip of his pen pointed, and the Letters came that January. Don’t read anything into that about your own state. Courts differ, and so do estates.

Telling people, the way the court wants it done

Once a hearing is set, the people with a stake in the estate have to be told. This is the step that trips up careful people, because the rules about how are stricter than anyone expects.

In California, you must give notice of the hearing to the person’s family members and to anyone who may have a right to some part of the estate. The court’s form for this is DE-121, Notice of Petition to Administer Estate, which tells them that the petition was filed, gives the date, time and place of the hearing, and explains what to do if they disagree with the petition.

Here’s the catch. California’s guide says another adult who is not a party to the case mails the notice. You can’t mail it yourself. A neighbor or a friend with no stake can do it, and the court will want proof that it happened the way the rules say.

California also requires you to arrange for the notice to be published in a newspaper of general circulation in the city where the person lived. The newspaper charges for it. You can be reimbursed from the estate later.

If the person died without a will, or the will leaves things to people you’ve never met, the list of who gets notice may be longer than you think. A cousin in another state. A stepchild the family lost touch with. Who counts is state law, so ask the clerk or a lawyer before you decide someone doesn’t need to hear from you.

Then let notice do its job. If someone objects to the petition, files something, or calls you angry about the will, you’ve moved out of self-help territory. A contested will is one of the clearest places in this book where I’d stop and hire a probate lawyer, paid from the estate where the court allows it. Don’t argue the will with relatives on the phone. Get the lawyer, and let the lawyer answer.

The hearing, and what the judge is deciding

At the California hearing, a judge decides whom to appoint as personal representative. The guide says you should attend in case the judge has questions. If there are no questions about the petition, the notice or the publication, the judge may grant the petition and appoint you.

Notice what’s being checked. Not whether you love the family, or whether you’ll do a good job. Whether the paperwork is complete, whether everyone was told the right way, and whether anything stands in the way. If a piece is missing, expect to be asked to fix it before anyone is appointed.

Afterward, California issues an Order for Probate, form DE-140, which states the court’s decision appointing you and lists your powers and responsibilities. Read that list. If you’re ever unsure whether you’re allowed to do something, the order is the first place to look, and the lawyer is the second.

Letters: the paper that opens doors

Then comes the document everyone will actually ask for.

California’s form is DE-150, titled plainly “Letters,” and the courts describe it as what an appointed representative uses to prove to others that the court has officially appointed them. Mine, from Ross County, were titled Letters of Authority. You’ll also see letters testamentary and letters of administration, depending on the state and on whether there’s a will. The name matters less than the job. Banks, brokerages, title companies and the motor vehicle office may each want this paper, often as a certified copy with the court’s seal, and not the will.

So count before you order.

Here’s my habit, since the Ross County window, and it’s only a habit. Start with every “yes” line on the authority check from Chapter 2, because each of those is an institution you’ll need to show authority to. Add the insurer for any property the estate owns. Add the title company or the recorder if there’s real estate to sell or transfer. Then add two for whatever you haven’t found yet, because you haven’t found it yet.

Then ask each institution two questions when you first call: do you need a certified copy, and do you keep it or send it back? Some will look and return it. Some will put it in a file and you’ll never see it again. Their answer changes your count.

Ask the clerk what certified copies cost, whether you can order more by mail later, and how long that takes. Write the answers on the court’s contact page. You may have a perfectly good reason to make a second trip one day. Running out shouldn’t be it.

Death certificates are a separate count from a separate office, and the series’ book on the first weeks after a death, named in the introduction, handles that one. Institutions often want both.

Bond, and when the court wants one anyway

A probate bond works roughly like insurance for the beneficiaries and creditors: if the representative mishandles the money, the bond is there to cover the loss. A court may require one before it issues Letters.

California Probate Code section 8481 sets out when a bond isn’t required there: when the will waives it, or when all the beneficiaries waive it in writing and those written waivers are attached to the petition, unless the will itself requires a bond. The same section adds the part people skip. Even with a waiver, the court may require a bond for good cause, either on its own or because an interested person asks, before or after Letters are issued.

So read the will for the word “bond.” Bev’s said none was required, and the court didn’t ask for one, but that’s her will and her court. If your will says nothing, or the beneficiaries don’t all agree to waive it, ask the clerk what your court expects, what a bond would cost and who pays for it. Better to learn it now than at the window.

Supervised or independent

This question changes your next six months more than any other in this chapter, and almost nobody asks it.

California has a law called the Independent Administration of Estates Act. Under Probate Code section 10450, the representative asks for that authority, either in the same petition that asks to appoint them or in a separate one, and can request full or limited authority. Under section 10500, a representative granted it may administer the estate without court supervision, within that law’s limits, but otherwise must handle the estate the same way as anyone else. The representative can still ask the court to supervise any particular action.

In plain terms: with independent authority, many ordinary steps don’t need a judge’s approval first. Without it, more of what you do waits on the court. Full and limited authority differ in what they let you do on your own, and your Order for Probate will say which you have.

Other states have their own versions of this idea, under their own names, and some don’t have it at all. Ask the clerk, before you file, whether your state offers a form of administration with less court supervision and what you’d need to request it. Ask again after the hearing which kind you received. If you have a lawyer, this is one of the first questions on the list.

If there’s no will

Without a will, you’re an administrator rather than an executor. California’s court glossary describes the administrator as the person, usually the spouse, domestic partner or a close relative, whom the court appoints to manage the estate of someone who died without one. The order of preference comes from state law, and Chapter 1 gave you California’s version.

The court process looks much the same: a petition, notice, a hearing and Letters. What changes is who inherits. With no will, your state’s intestate succession law decides that, and the heirs it names will be among the people you notify. Planning around intestacy is in Estate Planning for Beginners. Here you need only the list of heirs your state’s law produces, and if you aren’t sure who’s on it, a lawyer can tell you before you send a single notice.

The first court visit checklist

Take this with you the first time you go to the probate clerk’s window, or keep it in front of you on the phone. Next to each answer, note the date and who told you.

  1. The original will, or the clerk’s written confirmation that it has already been delivered, with the date.
  2. The person’s full legal name, last address, date of death and county of residence, exactly as they’ll appear on the petition.
  3. The names and mailing addresses of everyone who may need notice: the people named in the will, and the heirs your state’s law would name.
  4. Any written bond waivers from the beneficiaries, if the will doesn’t waive bond and they’re willing to sign.
  5. The filing fee, or a fee-waiver application. Ask whether the court takes a personal check.
  6. Ask: which petition form does this court use, and are there local forms on top of the state’s?
  7. Ask: who may mail notice, what proof of mailing do you want, and which newspaper do people use for publication?
  8. Ask: does this state offer administration with less court supervision, and how do I request it?
  9. Ask: what will my Letters be called, what does each certified copy cost, and can I order more by mail?
  10. Ask: what does the court expect me to file after appointment, and when?
  11. Ask: which of these filings has a deadline I can miss?

Number eleven is the one I’d ask even if I forgot the other ten. A clerk can’t tell you whether to file something. A clerk can usually tell you whether a date exists, and that’s the information that hurts most when you find it out late.

Before you file, hold everything in this chapter up against your own state. Read the probate pages your state court publishes for the public, then phone the county’s probate clerk and read your answers back. Where a clerk describes how the court runs, which form to use and when it’s due, the clerk is right and this book isn’t. Anything touching authority, liability or a disputed legal reading goes to the estate’s lawyer instead.

When the Letters come, write the date they were issued on the front of the folder. Every deadline from here on counts from a date like that one.

Count the copies twice.

Chapter 4: The First Thirty Days With Letters

“I’m sorry, Mrs. Calloway. We don’t have anything from you.”

It was Thursday, February 1, 2024, about twenty past ten in the morning, and the woman on the line worked for the second bank, the one out by the bypass, where Bev kept a savings account and not much else. Three weeks earlier I had mailed that bank a letter and a certified copy of my Letters of Authority, asking it to put the account in the estate’s name and tell me what else it needed. Now, as far as its computer knew, there was no letter, no copy and no me.

The phone log was open on the kitchen table, because by then it always was. I turned back to January and read her one line.

Wed., Jan. 10, 2024, 9:45 a.m. Second bank, savings ending 0371. Main number, transferred to the estate department. Man gave his first name and extension 4410. Said: mail a letter and one certified copy of the Letters to the department’s post office box, attention estate services, reference 24-0110-B on the letter. Mailed Thurs. the 11th by certified mail. Receipt stapled behind.

There was a pause long enough to hear her typing.

“Let me call you back.”

She did, at a quarter past two. The letter had been scanned into another department’s queue the day it arrived, my reference number printed right across the top, and had sat there for three weeks waiting for someone to notice it wasn’t theirs. Nobody had done anything wrong on purpose. A large organization had misplaced a piece of paper, which large organizations do every day. What turned it into one phone call instead of five was a line in a notebook that gave her a date, an extension and a number she could search for.

The Letters gave me the right to ask. The log is what made the asking stick.

What changed when the clerk handed you the envelope

For weeks you’ve been the person named in the will, and every bank, insurer and government office has told you, politely, that this means nothing to them. Then the clerk slides the court’s paper under the glass, you write the issue date on the front of the folder as Chapter 3 told you to, and the same people start taking your calls.

That’s the whole change, and it’s a big one. You can now ask institutions to deal with you about property the court has put in your care.

If the house still isn’t locked up, the mail isn’t reaching you, or nobody has told Social Security, that first-weeks work is covered in the series’ book on the first ninety days, and it comes before anything here. This chapter starts where the court’s authority does.

Before you call anyone, read two papers you already have. One is the court’s order appointing you, which in California is the Order for Probate from Chapter 3 and in your state may have another name. It lists what you’re allowed to do. The other is whatever tells you whether you have independent or supervised authority, which Chapter 3 told you to ask about. Those two decide how much of what follows you can do on your own and how much waits for a judge.

Authority isn’t permission to hurry

Here’s the feeling that arrives with the Letters, and I had it too: now that I’m allowed, I should get on with it. Close the accounts. Sell the car before the battery dies. Give Mom’s ring to the granddaughter who always admired it, because everybody agrees she should have it.

Don’t.

You’re still in the first of the three steps from the introduction, collecting. Nothing leaves the estate yet. Not money, not the car, not the ring, and not the fishing boat your brother says Dad promised him. “She would have wanted me to have this” is not a legal category, even when it’s true, and even when the “me” is you.

Leave the accounts open, too. An open account keeps producing statements, and statements are evidence. Chapter 5 gathers the money into one place in a sensible order. Closing things early, before you know what pays into them, is how a pension deposit bounces or an automatic payment you didn’t know about stops a policy.

Selling is a separate question with a sharper edge. Whether you can sell estate property without a judge signing off first depends on your state and on the kind of authority your order gives you. Read the order and the Letters first. If they don’t answer whether you may sell, ask the estate’s lawyer before you list anything, and write the answer down with the date and the name of whoever gave it.

Bills wait for Chapter 7. The exception is anything that keeps property from losing value: an insurance premium, a furnace repair in January, the electric bill that keeps the pipes from freezing. If something like that can’t wait, read your order again. If it doesn’t plainly cover the payment, ask the estate’s lawyer whether you have the authority and what you may pay it from. Note the answer and keep the receipt.

One institution at a time, in writing

Start with the authority check from Chapter 2. Every “yes” line on it is an institution holding property the court has now put in your hands. Those are your calls. The “no” lines stay on the outside-the-estate page, and the Letters don’t change that. A brokerage account that pays to your sister on death is still your sister’s business, whatever the court has said about you.

For each “yes” line, phone first. Ask where to send things, what they’ll need, and the keep-or-return question from Chapter 3. Ask, too, whether there’s an age limit on a certified copy they’ll accept, because a copy the court sealed in January may not satisfy someone in May.

Then put the request in a letter, even if the person on the phone says you don’t need to. A phone answer lasts as long as the call. A letter has a date on it, and you have a copy.

Keep the letter short. Who you are and that the court appointed you. The person’s full name and date of death. The account’s last four digits, never the whole number. A copy of your Letters, or a certified one if they said so. Then the asks, numbered so they can’t skip one:

  1. Please freeze this account or retitle it in the estate’s name, whichever your procedure requires, and tell me in writing which you’ve done.
  2. Please send all future statements and correspondence to me at the address below.
  3. Please tell me in writing the balance on the date of death.
  4. Please list anything else you need from me.

The third one is a favor to your future self. The inventory in Chapter 6 runs on date-of-death values, and it’s far easier to get that number now, while you’re already on the phone, than to circle back in three months.

Expect to be asked for a death certificate, your own ID, and sometimes the estate’s tax number before they’ll retitle anything. That number is Chapter 5. It’s fine to say you’ll have it within the week and ask them to freeze the account in the meantime. What isn’t fine is letting a helpful voice talk you into closing the account and mailing a check made out to the estate before the estate has anywhere to put it.

Now and then an institution won’t honor the Letters, or wants something you can’t produce, or keeps changing its answer. Ask for the refusal in writing. Then take it to the estate’s lawyer. A written no is something a lawyer can work with. A shrug on the phone isn’t.

Mail anything that encloses a certified copy in a way that gives you a receipt. That’s how my line on January 10 ended with “receipt stapled behind,” and why the woman at the second bank had something to search for.

Send it so you can prove it.

The insurance call, this week

The house is empty. The car hasn’t moved since the funeral. Both are insured in the name of someone who has died, and some of the most expensive surprises in this job begin right there.

Call the agent or the company this week. Say who died, that the court has appointed you, and that you’re sending your Letters. Bev’s insurer, as you saw in Chapter 3, held on to one of my certified copies before adding the estate to the policy. Yours may want something different. What an insurer needs from a fiduciary isn’t standard, so don’t guess at it and don’t rely on a cheerful “you’re fine” over the phone.

Ask these in writing and get the answers back in writing:

  1. Is the property covered today, and on what terms?
  2. Does the policy say anything about a house standing empty, and if so, what?
  3. Can the estate, or I as its representative, be named on the policy, and what do you need to do that?
  4. When is the next premium due, and where should the notice go?

Ask the same about the car. While you’re at it, take the keys off the hook by the door. A nephew offering to “keep the battery up” by driving it to work is a kind offer and an insurance question nobody wants to answer after a fender bender.

If the insurer says there’s no coverage, talks about canceling, or something has already happened, a pipe that froze or a window someone broke, call the estate’s lawyer that day. Property sitting uninsured in your care is exactly the kind of loss you’d someday have to explain to a judge or a beneficiary, and a lawyer can tell you what your state expects you to do about it.

Two IRS forms that do different jobs

The IRS needs to know you exist, too.

Form 56, Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship, is how you tell it. The IRS’s page for the form, last reviewed in August 2026, says it notifies the agency when a fiduciary relationship is created or ends. The instructions, revised June 2026, add the part that matters this month: generally, you file it when the relationship is created. They also say something worth reading twice. The IRS treats a fiduciary as if the fiduciary were the taxpayer, so the returns and the taxes due become yours to handle on the person’s behalf. Chapter 8 deals with what those returns are.

A few practical points from those same instructions:

You file a separate Form 56 for each person you act for. In practice that’s usually two. One names the person who died, for the final personal return. The other names the estate, which is a separate taxpayer.

The one for the person uses their Social Security number. The one for the estate uses the estate’s own tax number, which you won’t have until Chapter 5, so that form can wait a week or two.

If a court appointed you, will or no will, you attach your current Letters, or a court certificate, as proof.

It goes to the IRS service center where the person you’re acting for files returns. For the person who died, the Form 1040 instructions list that address.

You sign it under penalty of perjury. Read each line before you do.

Form 56 doesn’t change any address. Its instructions say so outright. For that, the IRS’s “Information for executors” page, last reviewed in September 2026, points to Form 8822, which changes the estate’s address of record. The person filing it must be the executor or someone with authority to act for the estate, and the IRS says that can include a fiduciary who has already submitted Form 56. It also says to allow 4 to 6 weeks for the change to go through.

Form 56 is not an address change, and Form 8822 is not a substitute for telling the IRS you’re the fiduciary. They do different jobs, so don’t assume one unlocks the other. If you’re acting on fiduciary status rather than on a court appointment, read both sets of instructions and work out whether the IRS wants the Form 56 in first. Either way, allow the four to six weeks, and expect letters to keep going to the old address until the change takes. One more reason the first-weeks mail work matters.

This is a book, not a tax preparer. If the person ran a business, had rental property, left unfiled returns, or the IRS was already writing to them before they died, bring in a CPA now rather than in March. Read the form’s instructions yourself either way. They’re short, and they’re the source.

The money notebook, now under oath

From the day you hold Letters, everything you write about money is heading toward a reckoning. California calls it the final account, and it can be waived if every person due a share signs a written waiver. Your state has its own version. That account gets built from what you record this month, not from what you remember next year.

The money notebook from the introduction doesn’t change shape. What changes is who may read it. Before, it was your own list. Now every page needs to make sense to a judge, a beneficiary, or a brother who has decided to be suspicious.

So write down everything. The certified mail receipt. The certified copies. The parking at the courthouse. If you think you might ask to be repaid for driving, write the miles and the reason for every trip on the day you make it. Whether your state allows mileage at all, and at what rate, is a question for the estate’s lawyer before you count on it.

My own habit was fifteen minutes every Sunday night, catching up the notebook and the log from the week, with the receipts in an envelope clipped inside the back cover. That’s my habit, not a rule. The rule underneath it is simpler. Nothing gets reconstructed later.

Write it the same day.

The institution log

The phone log you started with the introduction had four columns: when, who, what was said, and what they wanted back. From the day the Letters arrive, rule four more. Together the eight look like this:

  1. Date and time. The actual time, because “Tuesday morning” is useless in March.
  2. Who. A name, or at least a first name, plus the department and a direct line or extension.
  3. What they told you. One line, in their words where it matters.
  4. What they asked you to send. And by when, if they gave a date.
  5. Institution and account. Last four digits only. This page will sit on your kitchen table.
  6. What you sent or showed, and how. Letter, certified copy, in person, certified mail. Note whether they kept the certified copy.
  7. Reference number. Theirs, plus your mail receipt number if you have one.
  8. Follow-up date. When you’ll call if you hear nothing. When the item is finished, write “closed” and the date here instead.

Three habits keep the log honest. One line per contact, written that day, including the follow-up calls, which get their own lines rather than squeezed notes in the margin. Any line whose follow-up date has passed gets a phone call before anything else that morning. And if you couldn’t read a line aloud to a stranger and have them find your file, it isn’t finished yet.

That last test is the whole point. The woman at the second bank didn’t need my feelings about her bank. She needed a date, an extension and a reference number, in that order, and the log had them.

Before day thirty

Somewhere in this first month, hold what you’ve done up against your own state. The probate pages on your state court’s website will tell you what usually comes next. Then phone the county probate clerk and ask item ten from the Chapter 3 checklist a second time, in its appointed form: which filings are due from me now, and on what dates? Some of those dates may count from the issue date on the front of your folder. Your inventory deadline, in particular, is set locally, and Chapter 6 shows you how to meet it. Write the date the clerk gives you next to the Letters date, with the clerk’s name.

For local forms and filing dates, follow the court’s current written instructions and confirm them with the clerk. For what you’re allowed to do, what you could be held liable for, or two pieces of legal advice that don’t agree, stop and ask the estate’s lawyer.

The woman at the second bank called me once more that winter, in March, to say Bev’s savings account was in the estate’s name and the statements would come to me. It took her under a minute.

Log the callback.

Chapter 5: The EIN and the Estate Bank Account

The woman behind the desk at the bank downtown was perfectly nice about it.

It was a Tuesday morning, the sixteenth of January 2024, and I had come in with what I was sure was everything. The court’s Letters with the raised seal, Bev’s death certificate, my driver’s license, the white binder with Dale’s tabs in it.

She read the Letters all the way through, which I appreciated, and then she turned her monitor a quarter inch toward herself and said, “And do you have the tax ID for the estate?”

I said Bev’s Social Security number was on the death certificate.

“Not hers. The estate’s.”

I drove home. Forty minutes of driving, round trip, plus twenty in the lobby, for a conversation that could have happened on the telephone in four. That afternoon I applied online, printed the letter twice, and came back Thursday. The same woman opened the account in about half an hour and asked after the weather.

Nobody had done anything wrong. I just hadn’t understood a thing that the rest of this chapter exists to explain.

The estate is a taxpayer, and it isn’t you

Here’s the piece that reorders how you think about the next year.

Bev’s own last personal return still covers what she received up to the day she died. At death, the estate’s separate tax year also begins for post-death income. The IRS’s own instructions for Form 1041 put it plainly: for a decedent’s estate, the moment of death ends the person’s tax year and begins the estate’s. The estate is a separate entity for federal tax purposes, formed by the death itself.

Separate from her. Also separate from me.

That’s why her Social Security number wouldn’t do, and why mine would have been worse. A new taxpayer needs its own number, and for an estate that number is an EIN, an employer identification number. An EIN identifies the estate for federal tax purposes. It does not mean the estate has employees, though an estate that employs workers can have separate employment-tax obligations; ask the CPA about any worker the estate pays. The IRS page on filing an estate income tax return, last reviewed in April 2026, says it straight out: before you file an estate income tax return, you need a tax identification number for the estate. The Form 1041 instructions go further. Every estate required to file that return must have one.

Whether your estate will have to file is Chapter 8’s business, and the answer turns on how much income it takes in. But notice the order of operations, because it’s the trap. You find out whether you need to file a return months from now. Get the EIN promptly. A bank may require it before opening an estate account, so call the branch first and ask what it needs.

Get the number first. Sort out the return later.

Getting it: Form SS-4, free, and fast

The form is Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number. You can fill it out online and the IRS gives you the number at the end of the session, immediately, if the application goes through.

It costs nothing. I want to say that twice, because people lose money here. The IRS’s own page warns readers to beware of websites that charge for an EIN, and says you never have to pay a fee for one. If you search for this and land somewhere that wants forty dollars to “file your EIN,” close the tab. Go to irs.gov and start from there.

Now the practical traps, all from the IRS’s page on getting an EIN, last reviewed in August 2026, and the Form SS-4 instructions revised December 2025.

You get one session. The online application cannot be saved and resumed. It expires after fifteen minutes of inactivity and you start over. So don’t open it until you have the papers in front of you and twenty quiet minutes. I did mine at the kitchen table with the folder open and the phone face down.

The tool keeps hours. Eastern time: Monday through Friday from 6:00 a.m. until 1:00 a.m. the next day, Saturday from 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., and Sunday only from 6:00 p.m. to midnight. A government website with a closing time surprises people. Plan around it rather than discovering it at ten on a Sunday morning.

One a day. EINs are limited to one per responsible party per day, and the instructions add a detail that matters for us: for estates, that limit is applied to the person who died. One estate, one EIN, one day.

Apply once. If you think the session failed, stop and find out before you try again. An EIN, once assigned, is the entity’s permanent federal taxpayer identification number. The IRS page on no longer needing an EIN, last reviewed in November 2025, says it cannot be canceled. The agency can close the account, on a written request, but the number itself doesn’t go away. Two numbers for one estate is a mess you’d rather not make.

If you can’t use the online tool, Form SS-4 also goes in by fax or by mail, and the current instructions give the numbers and addresses. Expect it to take longer. Read the instructions for the method you choose, since they change.

The six lines on that form that are about you

Most of Form SS-4 is for businesses, and you’ll be writing “not applicable” more often than not. Six entries actually require a decision, and the instructions tell you what each one wants.
