The estate’s legal name goes on line 1. If the estate has no legal name of its own, the instructions say to enter the name of the person who died followed by the word “Estate.”

Line 3 is the care-of line. For an estate, that’s the executor, administrator or personal representative. Your name goes there, and the mailing address on the next lines is yours, not the empty house’s, because that’s the address the IRS will use.

Line 7 asks for the responsible party. For a decedent’s estate, the instructions name the executor, administrator, personal representative or other fiduciary, and the number beside it is your own Social Security number. Reading that line was the moment the job got personal for me, and I’d had the Letters for a week.

Line 9a is the entity type. You check Estate, and the number you enter in that space is the Social Security number of the person who died. This is where mine goes in and hers goes in, in two different boxes, for two different reasons.

Line 11 wants the date the business started or was acquired. For an estate, the instructions say to enter the date of death of the person named on line 1, or the date the estate was legally funded.

And line 12 asks for the closing month of your accounting year, which looks harmless and isn’t. December gives the estate a calendar year. Another month gives it a fiscal year. People agonize at that screen, so here’s the relief: the Form 1041 instructions say the executor chooses the estate’s tax period when filing its first income tax return. The first tax year may be any period of twelve months or less, ending on the last day of a month. The decision has real tax consequences for the beneficiaries, and it belongs to a CPA, not to a book and not to a dropdown. Chapter 8 gives you the question to ask. Ask it before that first return, not before this form.

Then you sign. The instructions say that for an estate the application is signed by the fiduciary, which is you.

One more thing, for the small number of readers it will save. If a return or a deposit comes due before the number arrives, the instructions say to write “Applied For” and the date you applied in the space for the number, and never to put a Social Security number there instead.

Print it twice

When the session finishes, the screen offers you the EIN confirmation letter. Print two copies and save the file somewhere you’ll find it.

One copy lives in the folder, behind the Letters. The other goes in the envelope you take to the bank, and you will be asked to hand it over.

Then write the number on the inside front cover of the money notebook, near where you keep the dates that matter. The nine-digit number identifies the estate to the federal government. You’ll be asked for it by a bank, a brokerage, an insurer, a CPA and at least one person on hold music.

Keep it where you can find it at eight at night.

The bank: call the branch first

Then open the account, and save yourself my Tuesday by telephoning the branch before you drive anywhere.

Ask what the bank requires to open a decedent’s estate checking account, and whether the branch you’re calling can do it or whether it goes to a department somewhere else. Ask whether an appointment is better. Ask who you’ll be sitting with. Then log it the way Chapter 4’s institution log wants it logged, with the name and the extension, because if the answer turns out to be wrong you want to know whose answer it was.

What they’ll want is some arrangement of five things: a certified copy of your Letters, the EIN confirmation letter, your own photo identification, the death certificate, and the estate’s mailing address. Banks differ on the details and on whether they keep a certified copy, which is why Chapter 3 told you to count more copies than you thought you needed.

While you’re there, settle five more questions and write the answers down.

Order checks, and look at what gets printed on them. You want the estate’s name on that line, not yours.

Ask about the monthly fee and the minimum balance, and ask what happens to both when the account sits at three hundred dollars for the last two months of the case.

Ask who is authorized to sign. For most estates that’s one person, which is you. If you’re serving with a co-executor, say so at the desk and find out what the bank requires of the two of you, because a bank’s rule and your court’s rule are separate things and you want them pointed the same direction.

Ask how statements come, and get them on paper if you have any choice. The final accounting at the end of this job is built out of statements, and a login you’ll forget is not a record.

And ask whether the bank wants Form 56 from you. If Chapter 4’s Form 56 applies to the estate, finish the estate copy after the EIN arrives; Chapter 4 has the instructions.

If a bank won’t open the account, ask for the reason in writing, then bring it to whoever is advising the estate. A written refusal is something a lawyer can act on, and some banks simply don’t do estate accounts at a branch counter.

Everything in, everything out, nothing personal

Now the rule that this whole chapter was built to deliver, and the only one in the book I’d put in capital letters if the publisher let me.

From the day that account opens, every dollar that belongs to the estate goes into it, and every dollar the estate pays goes out of it. Nothing personal touches it, in either direction, not once, not for an afternoon, not to be sorted out later.

Not your own money, lent to the estate to cover a bill you’re in a hurry about. Not the estate’s money, moved to your checking account because the transfer was easier than waiting for checks. Not the hundred dollars a cousin handed you at the funeral toward the headstone. Not a refund check you deposited at the drive-through on a Saturday without looking at the payee line.

Keeping the money separate is one of the four fiduciary duties from Chapter 1, borrowed from the CFPB’s guides. Of the four, it’s the one with the sharpest edge, because mixing the money is the mistake that converts a hard job into an accusation. Not because you stole anything. Because once the two sets of money have touched, there’s no document left that proves you didn’t, and the person asking the question in eight months may be a brother with a lawyer.

The test is a single question, and I used it for fourteen months: could a stranger, with the statements and the notebook and nothing else, see where every dollar came from and where it went?

If not, don’t do it.

Paying yourself back, the boring way

You’ve been out of pocket since before you were appointed. The filing fee, the certified copies, the certified mail. Chapter 1 told you to write down every dollar and the intro gave you the notebook; this is where that comes due.

Do it as its own transaction, visible on the statement. A check from the estate account, made out to you, with a line in the notebook that says what it repays and the date of the original payment, and the receipt filed behind it. One check per batch, or one per item if your state’s accounting is fussy, but never a withdrawal without a paper reason.

Never cash. Never a transfer with no note. Never netting it against money coming in, which is the quiet version of the same error: if a refund of $380 arrives and you’re owed $380, deposit the refund and write yourself a check. Two lines on the statement, not none.

And before you reimburse anything unusual, read the Chapter 1 ledger again. Reimbursement can depend on your state’s rules, on whether the expense was necessary, on documentation, on court approval, and on there being money left. California’s self-help guide says costs are typically repaid from the estate; typically is not always. When I had a payment I couldn’t classify, I asked Sam, who charged me for six minutes and saved me an argument.

If you’re ever unsure whether something is the estate’s expense or yours, pay it from your own pocket, document it, and ask before reimbursing. That order is reversible. The other one isn’t.

Moving the money in, in the right order

Now bring the estate’s cash together, and do it in an order that doesn’t break anything.

Start with the accounts marked yes on the Chapter 2 authority check. One at a time, with the letter and the date-of-death balance you already asked for in Chapter 4.

Take the plain ones first. A savings account in the person’s name alone, with nothing paying in and nothing paying out, closes cleanly and the money comes to the estate account. Good. Two lines in the log and move on.

Leave the checking account they actually used open for a while, and keep reading its statements. A pension deposit may still be coming. An automatic payment may still be going out, and one of them may be the insurance premium on the empty house. Chapter 4 told you not to close accounts early; this is the specific reason. You learn what pays in and out of an account by watching it for a cycle, not by asking the bank for a rundown.

A certificate of deposit may carry a penalty for early withdrawal, and it’s worth one phone call to find out whether it matures before you need the cash.

As for the dead person’s debit card, their autopay logins, and that recurring charge nobody recognizes: shut them down deliberately, one at a time, each with its own log line. Not in an afternoon of clicking.

Leave uncashed checks made out to the person who died alone until you’ve asked the bank what it will accept into the estate account and what it won’t. Rules differ, and tearing up the wrong check is permanent.

One last thing, and it’s why Chapter 8 exists. Any interest that account earns after the date of death is income of the estate, not of the person who died. A money market account with a real balance can generate enough of it to matter. So when the statement comes, note the interest in the notebook as the estate’s income, and keep that figure where your preparer can find it next spring.

The envelope, in order

Before you drive to the bank, put these in one envelope, in this order, so you’re not searching your coat pockets at the desk.

  1. A certified copy of your Letters, with the court’s raised seal. Ask on the phone whether the bank keeps it.
  2. The EIN confirmation letter. One of your two printed copies.
  3. A certified copy of the death certificate. Bring two if you have them to spare.
  4. Your own photo identification, and your Social Security number if you can recite it, because the bank is opening an account you will sign on.
  5. The estate’s mailing address in writing, exactly as you entered it on Form SS-4. Yours, not the empty house’s.
  6. The institution log and a pen. The answers you get at that desk are the ones you’ll be quoting in April.

Nothing else. No will, unless the bank asked for it on the phone. No binder of statements. A thin envelope and a short list of questions beats a briefcase every time.

When I got home from the second trip, Dale looked at the checkbook with the estate’s name printed on it and said, “Well, now she’s got a company.”

Which is about right. For the next fourteen months, Bev’s estate had a tax number, a bank account, an address and one employee who wasn’t being paid.

Keep that account clean and Chapter 11’s final accounting mostly writes itself.

Chapter 6: Finding Everything, and Writing It Down

I spent one Tuesday making eleven phone calls to find a single annuity of Bev’s.

Not a big one, in the end. Eleven thousand dollars and change, bought back in 1998 from an insurance agent whose office had long since become a nail salon downtown. I found it because a forwarded statement sat in the pile for three weeks before I opened it. If I hadn’t opened it, that annuity would simply not exist, as far as the court or anyone else was concerned.

The inventory is where you answer, in writing, under oath, what the estate owns. An omission may be an honest mistake, but a sworn filing still has to be corrected promptly under your court’s procedure. The job of this chapter is to lower the odds of needing to.

A snapshot, not a running total

Start with what the inventory actually is. It’s a sworn list of what the estate owned as of one date: the date of death. Not what it’s worth today, not what came in since, not what you’ve spent since. A photograph, not a video.

That matters because people drift into treating it as a kind of estate diary, updating it in their heads every time something changes, and then wondering why the paperwork never matches what they’re thinking. Keep the date fixed. Everything that belongs on this list belonged to the person the moment they died, no more and no less.

Where things hide

Most inventories are short on surprises and long on legwork. Here’s where the legwork finds things.

The last three years of tax returns. Not because the returns themselves are assets, but because every 1099 attached to them names an account, a brokerage, a pension administrator, or a payer you’d otherwise never think to call. Bev’s last return had a 1099-DIV from a brokerage I didn’t know she used.

The statements that keep arriving at the estate’s address of record. Chapter 4 told you to leave accounts open and watch what pays in and out of them. The forwarding itself, and the first few weeks of mail generally, are a different book’s territory. What I’m pointing at here is narrower: once the mail is reaching you, read every piece of it as a lead, not a chore. A dividend notice. A renewal letter. A premium due date. Each one names something, and each something is worth one phone call before you decide it’s nothing.

Bev’s forwarded mail is also how I found a magazine subscription, a loyalty account at a hardware store with four dollars of credit on it, and the annuity. Only the annuity belonged on the inventory. I read all three anyway, because I couldn’t tell which was which until I opened the envelope.

The safe deposit box. Banks handle access to a dead person’s box differently, and some want the Letters before they’ll let you in at all. Call first, and bring someone else along if your state wants a witness or an inventory of the box’s contents made on the spot.

The insurance declarations page. Not just the policy that pays a beneficiary, which Chapter 2 already told you isn’t the estate’s to manage, but anything that insures property the estate does own: the house, the car, a stamp collection that got its own rider in 2009.

The pension from the job in 1987. People change employers, employers change names, and pension administrators change again after that. If Bev’s 1099 hadn’t turned up a payer’s name, I wouldn’t have known to call.

The second bank from a town they left. Chapter 4’s second bank, out by the bypass, was the one that lost my letter. It existed at all because Bev had banked there in the 1990s and never quite closed the account when she moved.

The storage unit, the garage, the junk drawer. Not every asset is a piece of paper. A coin collection in a shoebox, a gun safe, a stack of savings bonds from a grandchild’s christening — these show up by looking, not by calling anyone. Walk the house once with a legal pad before anything gets moved or sorted, and write down what you see before you start deciding what to do with it. Bev’s storage unit held, among the expected boxes of linens, a coffee can of silver dollars that never once appeared on a bank statement.

Anyone who handled the person’s money before you did. A financial advisor, a tax preparer, a bookkeeper. They often know about an account or a policy that never generated a 1099 you’d have seen, because it hadn’t paid out yet. One phone call to Bev’s tax preparer from two years back turned up a second, smaller annuity I’d have missed entirely otherwise — the kind of find that makes the eleven calls for the first one feel almost efficient by comparison.

Searching for what nobody told you about

Some money belonging to an estate never sends a statement, because the institution holding it has already lost track of the owner.

There are two lanes here, and keeping them separate saves you from filing someone else’s money on the estate’s list.

The estate-asset searches you run yourself: each state’s unclaimed property office, indexed by USA.gov, for every state the person ever lived in, not just the one they died in. TreasuryDirect’s current savings-bond forms and claim instructions, for a lost, stolen, destroyed, or unredeemed bond — Treasury Hunt was discontinued September 30, 2025, so any book or website still sending you there is out of date. The FDIC and the NCUA, each of which keeps records of what happened to deposits if a bank or credit union in the person’s history failed. And the US Courts unclaimed funds locator, if bankruptcy ever touched their name.

The survivor-benefit searches belong elsewhere. Use The First 90 Days After a Parent Dies for PBGC pension, VA life-insurance, and other survivor-benefit searches. Bring every result back to Chapter 2’s authority check; include it here only if the governing paperwork and professional advice classify it as estate property.

I worked the list for Bev on a Sunday evening at the kitchen table, mostly expecting nothing. Ohio’s unclaimed property office had eighteen dollars from a closed utility deposit. Eighteen dollars. I reported it, because the rule I worked by was the plain one: report it if your state’s form and instructions require it; do not omit it merely because the amount is small or a relative claimed it.

Valuing what you find

Once you’ve found it, you need a number as of the date of death, and the method is not yours to pick freely. Use the valuation method your court requires.

California’s preliminary guide asks for a best estimate of date-of-death fair market value and does not require a formal appraisal at that stage, according to the California Courts self-help guidance on estimating the value of the estate. In formal probate there, the personal representative usually contacts a probate referee to value non-cash assets, which is why the Inventory and Appraisal separates what the representative valued from what the referee did. Other states order this differently.

So do not substitute a tax assessment or a trade-in figure unless the governing instructions or the appraiser says it is appropriate. A county tax assessment runs behind market value more often than it runs ahead, and a trade-in number is not necessarily what a car was worth the day somebody died. For a business interest, farm ground, a coin collection, anything with no public price, keep whoever valued it and their invoice with the inventory, because the court or the IRS may ask who valued it and how. The IRS uses fair market value at the date of death for gross-estate assets, which is a federal estate-tax principle and not by itself the filing rule for your state’s court form.

Ask the clerk for the current form, instructions, filing method, and deadline. Ask the estate’s lawyer which assets require a referee or a qualified appraiser and what valuation standard applies. Ask the CPA how the valuation will be used on tax returns.

Don’t guess at a value to save a phone call. An undervalued house looks careless at best and self-serving at worst, especially to a sibling who’s already watching for exactly that. An overvalued one can cost the estate money later, when it sells for less than the number you swore to. Get the real number, from someone qualified to give it, and keep the paper that shows how they got there.

If a business is involved — even a small one, even one that’s basically a truck and a client list — stop and call a lawyer or a CPA before you put any number on the inventory at all. Valuing a business the person owned alone is a different, harder problem than valuing a house, and it’s not one this book will walk you through.

Filing it

California’s version is the Inventory and Appraisal, form DE-160, filed with the probate court. It’s the named example in this book because California publishes its process clearly; your state’s form will carry a different name and the same purpose.

What it won’t carry, anywhere, is a single national deadline. I can’t give you one, and any book that does is guessing. Ask your clerk when the inventory is due in your case, write the date on the front of the folder the way Chapter 3 had you write the Letters’ date, and treat it the way you’d treat a tax deadline: on the calendar, not in your head.

When something turns up later

It will. An old annuity, a second will drawer nobody searched, a dividend check from a company that merged twice since the statement was mailed.

You don’t start over. You amend. The procedure for amending an inventory is set by your court, and it exists precisely because nobody finds everything the first time. Call the clerk, ask what an amendment requires in your case, and add the item — late is not the same as wrong, as long as you correct it once you know.

What stays off the list, and why you track it anyway

Put on the filed inventory exactly what your state’s form, instructions, order, and lawyer require. Do not assume every item that bypasses probate is omitted everywhere; court inventories and reporting requirements are set state by state, and characterization questions are not safely settled by a rule of thumb from a book. Chapter 2’s authority check tells you what you have power over. It does not tell your court what belongs on its form.

Keep a separate private tax-information list for assets not reported on the court form. Not for the court. For yourself, and for Chapters 8 and 9, which need to know what the estate owned in the broadest sense long before either tax chapter cares whether the court had authority over it.

The paper trail hunt

Fourteen places to look, roughly in the order that finds the most for the least driving:

  1. The last three years of tax returns and every 1099 attached to them.
  2. Mail reaching the estate’s current mailing address, each piece opened and read.
  3. The checkbook or check register, if one exists, for account numbers you haven’t matched yet.
  4. The safe deposit box.
  5. Insurance declarations pages, filed by company, not by policy number you don’t have yet.
  6. A former employer’s benefits office, for any pension or retirement account.
  7. Any account statement older than a year, which sometimes shows an account that closed since.
  8. The county recorder’s office, for deeds in the person’s name.
  9. The county assessor, for a property tax bill that names an owner you didn’t expect.
  10. The state’s unclaimed property office, for every state they lived in.
  11. TreasuryDirect, for any savings bond that is missing or was never cashed. Use the site’s current claim route, not the retired search tool.
  12. The FDIC and NCUA, if a bank or credit union in their history failed.
  13. The federal courts’ locator for money left behind in a closed bankruptcy case.
  14. Anyone who knew them well enough to ask, “Did she ever mention a second account, or a box somewhere?”

Work it once, in order, before you file. Then expect to amend anyway.

What the inventory is not

It is not a guess, and it is not a negotiation. I’ve heard of executors who left an item off on purpose because a sibling claimed it loudly and often, figuring it was easier to let the argument happen off the books than on it. Don’t. The inventory is sworn, and the Ohio-deposit rule above still governs: a loud claim from a relative is not a reason to leave an item off a form that requires it. Chapter 10 handles who gets it after that, not Chapter 6.

It’s also not the place to settle whether something is the estate’s in the first place. That question belongs to the Chapter 2 authority check, and if a line there still says unclear, it stays unclear here too — sent to counsel, not guessed at because the inventory deadline is close.

Dale asked me, the week I made those eleven calls, why I didn’t just let the small one go. I told him it wasn’t about the eleven thousand dollars. It was about the one call I hadn’t made yet.

Make it.

Chapter 7: Bills, Claims and the Word “No”

The hospital bill for Bev came in late March 2024, four months after we buried her, in a window envelope with a barcode along the bottom edge.

I was standing at the kitchen counter. I had the checkbook for our joint account out of the drawer before I’d finished reading the second line, because that is what thirty years of paying bills on time does to a person. Pen uncapped. Date written.

Dale came in for his thermos and looked at the envelope, then at the checkbook.

“Whose bill is that?”

Three words into my answer I stopped, put the pen down, and went to find the folder instead. That thirty seconds is the reason this chapter exists.

The estate owes it. You usually don’t

Start with the rule, because everything else in this chapter is a wrinkle in it.

A person’s debts don’t vanish when they die. According to the FTC’s consumer page “Debts and Deceased Relatives,” dated February 2023, those debts are owed by and paid from the dead person’s estate, and by law family members usually don’t have to pay them out of their own money. The FTC also says plainly that if there isn’t enough money in the estate to cover a debt, it usually goes unpaid.

The CFPB’s current list of exceptions is longer than a quick summary suggests, and you should read it as a short checklist against your own situation rather than as background. You may be personally responsible if you cosigned the obligation, or if you’re a joint credit-card account holder rather than merely an authorized user. You may be responsible as a surviving spouse where your state’s law imposes responsibility for that specific debt, or as an executor or administrator where state law reaches property jointly owned with a spouse. You may also be responsible as a surviving spouse where applicable community-property law reaches property you held jointly. If you match any of these, take the contract and statements to a local probate or consumer lawyer before paying anything.

Read that last one twice. It’s about you, in your job, this year. Everything that follows is built to keep you out of it.

Being the one who settles the debts is a different thing from owing them. The person currently authorized by the court or another valid state process handles estate debts; being named in the will alone does not supply that authority. Where there’s no will, a court may appoint an administrator, a personal representative or a universal successor and give them that power, and in some states another process can make someone the estate’s representative without a formal court appointment.

That hospital bill was Bev’s. It was never mine. The envelope didn’t know that, and neither did I, for about half a minute.

Telling creditors you’re here

Your state may require publication for unidentified creditors and a separate, prescribed notice to known or reasonably ascertainable creditors. These are the legal notice steps, not the only ways a creditor may hear about a death.

California is the worked example this book keeps coming back to, and its formal-probate overview is blunt about the duty. The personal representative must give formal notice to creditors using the Notice of Administration to Creditors, form DE-157. The California Courts self-help description of that form says it tells creditors who has been appointed, that the representative has started managing the estate, how and when to make a claim, and what may happen if they don’t file a claim on time.

Those last two parts matter more than the rest. A notice that starts a clock is only useful to you if you know what the clock says.

And here I have to disappoint you, deliberately. There is no national creditor-claim window. I looked for one that I could stand behind in print, from an official source, and it does not exist, because the period is set by state law and the periods differ. Some are counted from the day notice is published. Some run from the day a known creditor is actually notified. Some run from the appointment. A book that hands you one number for all fifty states is guessing, and the consequence of a wrong guess lands on the person holding the Letters.

So the number comes from two places, and neither of them is me. Read the current probate pages your own state’s courts publish. Then confirm what you read with the clerk’s office handling your case. Ask for the claim period, ask what starts it running, and ask what form the notice takes where you are. Write the answer and the date beside it in the folder.

The second half of the notice job is the known creditors. Publishing in a newspaper reaches the creditor you’ve never heard of. It does nothing useful for the card company whose statement is sitting in your mail pile with the account number printed on it. Those you notify directly, by the method your state prescribes, and you keep proof you did it. Every one of them goes in the institution log from Chapter 4, with the date mailed and the receipt number stapled behind.

Why the first bill shouldn’t be paid first

The instinct that had me reaching for a checkbook is the single most expensive instinct in this job.

Here’s the shape of the problem. Bills arrive in the order the postal service delivers them, which has nothing to do with the order the law says they get paid. Pay the one that arrived Tuesday, and you may have spent money that a different claim was legally entitled to. If the estate later runs short, the creditor who should have been paid is not going to take “it came in first” as an answer, and the FTC’s fourth exception is sitting right there.

So the sequence is: collect, learn, then pay. Collect every bill and claim into one place. Learn your state’s rules on timing and ranking. Then pay, in whatever order the law and the court set.

Collecting is the easy part and it starts today. Every bill, statement, collection letter and demand goes in one envelope, unpaid, in the order it arrived, with the date you received it written in the top corner in pencil. Nothing gets thrown out, including the ones you’re sure are wrong. The ones you’re sure are wrong are often the most important to keep.

Some payments, though, cannot wait for the whole claim period to run, and a flat “pay nothing” rule would be its own kind of malpractice. The house insurance renews. The court wants its filing fee. The lawyer and the appraiser send invoices for work that keeps the case moving. State law may permit or require certain categories to be paid earlier, and the categories vary. Those are authority questions, not procedure questions, which puts them where Chapter 4 put every authority question: in front of the estate’s lawyer, with the court’s order and your Letters on the desk. The clerk can tell you which form and what deadline. The clerk cannot tell you that a payment is safe.

Ask before you pay.

Making a claim prove itself

A bill in an envelope is an assertion, not a fact. You’re allowed to ask it to prove itself, and in dealing with debt collectors you have specific federal rights while you do.

Ask one threshold question before any of this applies: is this an FDCPA-covered debt collector — a collection agency, debt buyer or collection lawyer — rather than the original creditor billing you directly? The federal rules below generally cover collectors handling personal, family or household debt; they generally don’t cover the original hospital or lender, and they don’t cover business debt. For an original creditor, request documentation anyway, but don’t expect the federal clock to apply, and check your state’s own rules.

When a covered collector is involved, the FTC sets out who it may even discuss a dead person’s debt with. The spouse. The parents of a deceased minor child. A legal guardian, the lawyer, and the executor or administrator or personal representative with power to pay debts from the estate. A confirmed successor in interest. Anyone else, the FTC says, the collector may not discuss the debt with at all. Collectors may contact other relatives, usually once, only to get the representative’s contact details, and may not discuss the debt with them.

Which means that when your cousin calls to say a collector phoned her about Bev’s card, the collector has already stepped past a line. Tell your cousin to give them your name and nothing else.

The FTC also says a covered collector generally has to give you validation information about the debt, either during its first phone call with you or in writing within five days after first contacting you, subject to the regulation’s exceptions. That information includes who the collector is, how much is owed broken out into interest, fees, payments and credits, and the name of the creditor. It also includes what to do if you don’t think it’s your debt, and your debt collection rights. The same page says collectors can’t contact you before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. unless you agree to it.

Then the part I’d tattoo on the inside of the folder. It comes from the CFPB’s page “Am I responsible for my spouse’s debts after they die?”, last modified September 22, 2026. Dispute a debt in writing within 30 days of the validation notice, and the collector must stop contacting you until it verifies the debt in writing.

In writing. Within thirty days. Not a phone call where a pleasant person agrees with you and makes a note.

What you’re asking for, in practical terms, is the account history: when the account opened, what it was for, what was charged and when, what was paid, and how the number on your envelope was arrived at. Twice in Bev’s estate that request produced a smaller number than the one first demanded. Once it produced nothing at all, and I never heard from that company again.

Who gets paid first is not yours to decide

When there’s enough money for everybody, the ranking question never comes up. When there isn’t, it is the whole game.

Priority classes and their caps are state law. I’m not printing a list of classes, and I’m not printing an order, not even as a rough shape, because I couldn’t verify one that holds nationally and a plausible-sounding wrong order is worse than no order at all. Get the current statute, or get written advice from the estate’s lawyer, before you pay competing claims. That instruction is the content. There isn’t a shortcut hiding behind it.

California’s formal-probate overview puts the condition in six words that are easy to skate past: if there is money to pay the estate’s debts, the representative will pay the debts from the estate. The whole chapter lives in that “if.”

When there isn’t enough

This is the clearest stop-and-hire-a-lawyer moment in this book, and I’d rather say so at the top of the section than bury it at the bottom.

If the claims against the estate look like they may exceed what the estate holds, stop paying anything that isn’t already authorized, and get a probate lawyer engaged, paid from estate funds where your court allows it. Not a consultation someday. This week.

The reason is arithmetic plus exposure. The CFPB says that if there is no money or property left in an estate, or the estate can’t pay, the debt generally goes unpaid. It gives the example of a state whose law requires the estate to pay survivors first, leaving nothing for debts. So an insolvent estate is a known situation with a legal shape, not a disaster you caused. But the FTC’s fourth exception means the person who hands out that insufficient money in the wrong order can end up personally on the hook. The estate’s insolvency is not your fault. Mishandling it could be your bill.

You’ll also meet claims in this zone that are nothing like a credit card. State Medicaid programs may seek recovery against an estate after a death, and the rules and the exceptions belong to each state’s Medicaid agency. If a notice of that kind arrives, send it to the lawyer and call the agency named on the letter, rather than deciding on your own what it means.

A thin estate is the one job in this book I would not do alone.

The calls that start after the obituary

Bev’s obituary ran in the paper, as obituaries do, and the calls started inside two weeks.

The CFPB has a page on exactly this, “Is it a scam if a debt collector calls me after seeing my relative’s obituary?”, last reviewed September 24, 2024. It says some scammers read obituaries and other legal notices, then contact relatives posing as debt collectors to collect money or harvest personal information for identity theft. Its practical test is the one I used. A legitimate collector generally has to give you details about the debt in the first conversation or within five days. If a caller knows you’re the personal representative and still won’t give you those details, the CFPB says you may be dealing with a scam.

The CFPB’s other instruction is the one to repeat out loud before you answer the phone this week. Don’t give anyone your Social Security number, your date of birth or financial account numbers unless you know who you’re dealing with.

I developed one sentence for those calls and used it maybe a dozen times. “Send it to me in writing at the estate’s address, and I’ll look at it.” Then I hung up. Nobody who was real ever objected, and most of the others never wrote.

The three that keep running

While you’re collecting and learning, three categories do not pause politely to wait for you.

A mortgage on a house the estate holds keeps accruing, and the lender’s rights in that house are a different animal from an unsecured claim. A car loan does the same. Utilities on a property the estate is responsible for keep the pipes from freezing and the sump pump running, and letting them lapse can turn a house into a smaller asset in one cold week.

None of that makes paying them automatically your call. It makes them the first things on the list you take to the lawyer, with the question phrased as authority rather than advice: do I have the power, under the order appointing me and my state’s law, to keep these current, and from which funds. Get the answer in writing if you can, and write the date beside it either way.

Bev’s house sat empty and insured through that winter, and the heat stayed on at fifty-five degrees the whole time. For Bev’s estate, Sam confirmed that keeping the heat at fifty-five degrees was an authorized property-preservation expense, paid from the estate account.

The claim triage sheet

One page per bill. Five questions, in this order, before any money moves.

  1. Whose debt is it? The dead person’s, a joint debt, or one of the CFPB’s exceptions that could make it personally yours. If it’s possibly yours, that goes to the lawyer before anything else happens.
  2. Who is asking, and have they proven the debt? First note whether this is an FDCPA-covered collector or the original creditor. For a covered collector, note whether validation information arrived on first contact or in writing within five days, and the date you sent any written dispute, counting the thirty days.
  3. What kind of claim is it? Secured against specific property, an expense of administering the estate, a tax, or an ordinary unsecured claim. Write what you think and underline the word “think.”
  4. Did this creditor get proper notice, and when does the state’s claim period end for it? Enter the date the clerk or the lawyer gave you, with their name beside it.
  5. Who authorized payment, and from where? A court order, written advice from the estate’s lawyer, or nothing yet. If it’s nothing yet, the bill goes back in the envelope.

The decision rule has one line. Do not pay ordinary unsecured claims until you’ve identified your state’s claim deadline and its priority rules, and continue only those payments that a court or a professional has confirmed: administration costs, taxes, secured obligations, and what’s needed to preserve property.

Keep the sheets in the order the bills arrived. When the lawyer asks what’s outstanding, you hand over the stack instead of reconstructing four months from memory.

What happened to Bev’s bill

I called the hospital’s billing office the day after Dale asked his question, told them I was the appointed personal representative, gave them the estate’s mailing address, and asked for the account history in writing.

It came in nine days. Two of the charges had already been covered and the balance was smaller than the first notice said. I took the corrected statement to Sam, who looked at it for less time than it took me to explain it, told me where it sat among Bev’s other claims, and said to pay it from the estate account once the claim period had run.

So I did, months later, with a check that had the estate’s name printed on it.

The money came out the same either way. What would have been different is who paid it, what I could prove, and whether a creditor with a better claim had a reason to come looking for me afterward.

Put the pen down first.

Chapter 8: The Final Return and the Estate Income-Tax Return You May Need

Sam had a folder on his desk with a sticky note that just said “TWO RETURNS,” in block letters, underlined twice.

“People hear ‘taxes’ and think one form,” he told me, somewhere in the second month of Bev’s estate. “There are two different taxpayers here. Bev, for the part of the year she was alive. And the estate, for everything that happened to her money after she wasn’t.”

I wrote that down. Then I asked which one I was supposed to do first, and he said “both, eventually, and not the same way,” which was not the answer I wanted that morning.

Two taxpayers, two returns

Keep the two returns on separate lines in the folder.

The first return is the decedent’s own final income tax return — Form 1040 or 1040-SR, the same form they’d have filed if they’d lived the whole year. The IRS’s instructions for this are direct: prepare it the way you’d prepare it if the person were alive, reporting income only up to the date of death. If prior years went unfiled, those may be owed too, and you’ll want to know that early rather than finding out from a notice.

The second return, if the estate needs one, is the estate’s own income tax return, Form 1041. That’s a different return for a different taxpayer. The estate is a separate legal entity from the person who died and from you, the way Chapter 5 explained when you got its EIN. It files its own return, under its own name and its own number, for the income it earned after death — interest on the account you opened, dividends that kept arriving, rent on a house still sitting in the estate’s name.

Different forms. Different taxpayers. Put each deadline on the calendar separately. If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember that the sticky note was right.

The final 1040: finishing what Bev started

The final personal return covers January 1 through the date of death, same deductions and credits available, same forms used for whatever kind of income she had. The person preparing it — you, or more likely a CPA working from your folder — treats it exactly like an ordinary return for a year that happened to end early.

One complication worth expecting: interest and dividend statements. A payer may not split a 1099 at the date of death. A Form 1099-INT or 1099-DIV issued in the decedent’s name may lump together interest or dividends earned before death with interest or dividends earned after death that actually belongs on the estate’s return. The preparer reports the full amount on the decedent’s final return, subtotals it, then backs out the portion that belongs to the estate and notes where it’s going instead. IRS Publication 559 — the agency’s own guide for people doing exactly this job — includes a worksheet built for reconciling those split amounts between the two returns. If your CPA mentions “nominee income” or asks for every 1099 issued in Bev’s name for the year she died, this is why.

If there’s a refund coming on that final return, it’s often claimed with Form 1310, the Statement of Person Claiming Refund Due a Deceased Taxpayer. There’s a practical trap in it: a refund check can come back made out to someone who’s no longer here to deposit it, and sorting that out with the bank is one more reason an estate account stays open longer than you planned for. If a refund is due, have the preparer check the current Form 1310 instructions. The IRS uses Form 1310 for many refund claims after a death, but the required paperwork depends on who is filing and whether the court appointed a personal representative.

Does the estate need its own return?

Not every estate does. The question has a real answer, and the answer lives in the current Form 1041 instructions, not in a general impression someone has from a different year’s estate.

For the 2025 tax year, the IRS’s instructions for Form 1041 set out three filing triggers for a domestic estate. Gross income of $600 or more for the tax year is one. A beneficiary who is a nonresident alien is another. Holding a qualifying investment in a qualified opportunity fund during the year is the third. Any one of the three is enough on its own to require a return. Because the test is gross income rather than net income, check every source of post-death income against the threshold — a single year of interest on an ordinary savings account can clear it.

Here’s the part I want you to sit with for a second. These instructions get reissued every year, and the rules inside them can shift. The IRS’s own summary page for executors still gets quoted as saying “more than $600” with no other conditions. That isn’t quite what the current instructions say once you add the nonresident-alien trigger and the opportunity-fund trigger. Have whoever prepares the estate’s return check the current year’s Form 1041 instructions directly, not a page remembered from a prior filing season or a summary written for a different year. A rule that was accurate two years ago can be incomplete this year, and nobody wants to find that out from a notice instead of from a preparer.

When it’s due, and what buys you time

A calendar-year estate, running January to December, files Form 1041 and the attached Schedules K-1 by April 15 of the following year. A fiscal-year estate files by the 15th day of the fourth month after its tax year closes. Have the CPA identify the estate’s actual closing date before calendaring the return.

For a nonbankruptcy estate, a timely Form 7004 provides an automatic five-and-a-half-month filing extension, an easy number to misremember and an easy one to get burned by if a deadline matters down to the day. And an extension to file is not an extension to pay. The IRS charges interest on tax that isn’t paid by the regular due date whether or not you filed for more time to get the paperwork together.

If the estate expects to owe tax year over year, it may also need to make estimated payments, the same way a person with income outside a paycheck does. That’s a calculation, not a guess, and it belongs with whoever is doing the return.

The decision nobody tells you is a decision

Somewhere in opening the estate’s first return, someone has to pick its accounting period. Calendar year, matching January to December, is one option, and it’s the one a reader can pick without noticing a choice was made. A fiscal year is the alternative, within the limits line 12 of the SS-4 already put in front of you in Chapter 5. The Form 1041 instructions say the executor makes that initial choice with the estate’s first income-tax return, and that a later change of accounting period requires Form 1128. So it is a choice, not a lock, but changing it is its own filing. This is a CPA’s question, not a form to fill in on your own on a Sunday night.

Why would anyone pick anything else? Timing income and deductions across two different tax years can change what gets taxed when, sometimes meaningfully. This is exactly the kind of choice that looks like a dropdown menu and is actually a real decision with real consequences down the road. Bring it up in your first conversation, not your last.

The estate also needs its own EIN before any of this starts, which Chapter 5 already walked you through. If you skipped straight to this chapter because taxes felt urgent, go back. Apply for the estate’s EIN promptly. A required Form 1041 uses the estate’s EIN; if it has not arrived by the filing deadline, have the preparer follow the current Form 1041 instructions for an EIN that is still pending.

What the estate owes beneficiaries: the K-1 surprise

If the estate distributes income to beneficiaries during the year, each of those beneficiaries gets a Schedule K-1 showing their share of what the estate earned and passed through to them. They report that income on their own personal returns.

Say that out loud to the people on your distribution list well before it happens. Your brother who received a check may later receive a Schedule K-1 reporting income he may need to include on his own return. Tell beneficiaries that before the distribution; the CPA can explain what their K-1 means.

The mechanics behind it are simpler than the form looks. An estate generally gets to deduct the income it distributes to beneficiaries from its own taxable income, up to a limit tied to what the estate actually earned that year. The beneficiary then picks up that same income on their own return instead. The deduction exists so the same dollar isn’t taxed in both places, and the K-1 is how the IRS tracks whose return it landed on. If the estate holds income back instead of distributing it — saving it for a later court-approved distribution, say — the estate itself owes the tax on what it kept. That’s one more reason the timing of a distribution isn’t only a family question. It’s a tax question too, and it belongs on the same list you take to the CPA.

Publication 559 is free, and it’s actually useful

The IRS publishes a guide written for exactly the job you’re doing — Publication 559, Survivors, Executors, and Administrators. It isn’t dense tax-code language aimed at a preparer; it’s aimed at the person holding the Letters. It includes a checklist of forms a personal representative might need, organized by due date, and the same worksheet mentioned earlier for splitting 1099 amounts between the decedent’s final return and the estate’s return.

Download it, print the checklist page, and put it in the folder. It won’t replace a CPA for anything complicated, but it will tell you what questions exist before you’ve thought to ask them.

The twelve questions for the CPA

Sam’s six-minute increments taught me something: a good professional’s time is wasted on vague questions and well spent on specific ones. So before your first meeting about the estate’s income taxes, write these down and bring the sheet with you.

  1. Does this estate need to file Form 1041 at all, under this year’s current instructions?
  2. What’s our gross income for the year so far, and does it clear the filing threshold?
  3. Should we pick a calendar year or a fiscal year, and what difference would it make for this specific estate?
  4. Is there unreported income from a prior year the decedent didn’t file?
  5. Which 1099s need to be split between the final 1040 and the estate’s 1041, and by how much?
  6. Is a refund due on the final return, and does Form 1310 need to go with it?
  7. Will the estate owe estimated tax payments during the year, and on what schedule?
  8. Do we need to file Form 7004 for more time, and does that change what’s due by the original deadline?
  9. If we distribute to beneficiaries this year, what will their K-1s likely show, and when should I warn them?
  10. Are there any unfiled prior-year returns for the decedent I don’t know about yet?
  11. What records do you need from me, and in what format, before our next meeting?
  12. What’s the one thing about this estate’s taxes that worries you most, that I haven’t asked about?

Hand the sheet over on paper. Let the CPA answer in whatever order makes sense to them. A written question list can make that hour more useful and may help prevent avoidable amendments.

What Sam actually meant

Back to that sticky note. What Sam meant, once I understood it, wasn’t complicated: Bev’s life and Bev’s estate are not the same taxpayer, even though they share a name and a shoebox of paperwork. Her final individual return still accounts for income through the date of death. The estate accounts for its own post-death income under a separate taxpayer number.

Getting that distinction straight in your head early is worth more than any form in this chapter. The forms, your CPA can walk you through. The idea that there are two taxpayers, each with its own deadline to put on the calendar — that’s the part you have to bring to the first meeting yourself.

Chapter 9: Estate Tax — Probably Not You, But Read This Anyway

Sam had Bev’s folder open on his desk, and I asked him the question I’d been putting off since January.

“Does she owe estate tax?”

He didn’t open a book. He didn’t even reach for his yellow pad. “Add up what she had. Then I’ll tell you in about ten minutes whether you need to worry about this chapter at all.” He was right about the ten minutes. He was right about the rest of it too — for most estates, this is the shortest chapter in the folder.

The number, and the three things you add before you use it

Here’s the number first. For deaths in 2026, the IRS’s federal estate tax filing threshold is $15,000,000. For deaths in 2025, it was $13,990,000. Both figures come from the current Instructions for Form 706.

But the number alone isn’t the test, and this is where a lot of kitchen-table arithmetic goes wrong. For a US citizen or resident who dies in 2026, Form 706 is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and specific exemption exceeds $15,000,000, or when the executor elects portability regardless of estate size. Three things get added together before the comparison happens. Add only the first one and you can talk yourself out of a filing you owe.

Adjusted taxable gifts is the one nobody sees coming. Large gifts made during the person’s lifetime can come back into this calculation years later, and the Form 706 instructions expect reasonable efforts to identify them. There’s a section near the end of this chapter on how to find out whether any were made. Read it before you decide this chapter doesn’t apply to you.

Notice what that threshold tracks: the year someone died, not the year you happen to be filing the paperwork. If your mother died in November of 2025 and you’re sorting through this in March of 2026, her estate is measured against the 2025 number, not the 2026 one. Write the date of death on the folder next to the threshold you’re checking it against, so nobody down the line confuses the two.

For an estate like Bev’s, the number sits so far above what she actually owned that the conversation ends there. A paid-off house, a car, a few accounts, a small annuity nobody remembered: that total didn’t get near fifteen million dollars. If that’s your situation, read the rest of this chapter anyway, because two paragraphs in it might still apply to you even when the tax itself never will.

What actually gets counted

The threshold only means something once you know what goes into the pile being measured against it. The IRS counts the gross estate: essentially everything the person owned, or held certain interests in, valued at fair market value on the date of death. Bank accounts, real estate, investments.

And some things that never pass through probate at all. The gross estate may include certain life-insurance proceeds and trust interests even when they pass outside probate. Have an estate-tax professional classify each policy and trust under the current Form 706 instructions. Whether a particular policy counts turns on details like who the proceeds benefit and what control the person kept over the policy — which is a reading job, not a guess.

So an estate that looks comfortably “under the limit” using the house and the checking account can look different once a policy or an old trust gets classified and added in. It’s one more reason the valuation work from Chapter 6 isn’t only about the court’s inventory — the same numbers feed this chapter’s test.

The clock that starts without telling you

If an estate does need to file, the form is Form 706, and its deadline is the tightest one anywhere in this book: generally nine months after the date of death. A timely Form 4768 requests an automatic six-month extension to file. It does not extend the time to pay; pay the estimated tax by the original due date unless the IRS grants a separate payment extension. Chapter 8 said the same thing about Form 1041, and it’s just as true here.

Nine months sounds like a lot of time in the first week. It doesn’t sound like a lot of time once you’ve spent three of those months waiting on a single institution’s written answer about what an account is actually worth. If there is any chance this chapter applies to your estate, that clock starts on the date of death, and it starts whether or not you’ve found it yet.

Portability: the paragraph that might pay for this book

Here’s the scenario that makes this chapter worth reading even for a modest estate: your parent died survived by a spouse.

The executor of the first spouse’s estate can elect portability on Form 706, making that spouse’s unused exclusion available to the survivor. The IRS calls it the deceased spouse’s unused exclusion amount. Note who does the electing: it’s the executor of the estate of the person who died first, on that estate’s return, not something the survivor files on their own later. Which means an estate that owes no tax at all, and wasn’t otherwise required to file, might still need a return filed — so the surviving spouse carries the unused exclusion forward.

The ordinary deadline is the same Form 706 due date described above, with the same extension rules. But if that deadline is missed and the estate wasn’t otherwise required to file, there’s a second door. A simplified late-election procedure can reach all the way to the fifth anniversary of the date of death, under the IRS’s Revenue Procedure 2022-32. It isn’t automatic. It isn’t something to attempt without an estate-tax professional reading the current procedure with you.

The return made under that procedure has to say, right at the top, that it’s being filed under this specific relief — a line only a professional should be drafting. If your situation is “a surviving spouse, and we never filed anything,” that sentence is the reason to pick up the phone today rather than next month.

Portability is one reason an estate below the filing threshold may file Form 706 even when no estate tax is due. Nobody owes a dollar of tax. The filing itself is the point — it locks in a number the surviving spouse might need years later, at a death nobody is thinking about yet.

What closes a case, and what doesn’t

A beneficiary may eventually ask you for an estate tax closing letter — proof, in their mind, that everything is settled. Here’s the honest answer in two parts.

First, the letter exists only where a Form 706 or Form 706-NA was actually filed, even in cases where no tax ends up being owed. It is never issued for a Form 1041, the estate’s income tax return from Chapter 8. If nobody filed a Form 706 for your estate because nobody had to, there is no closing letter coming. That isn’t an oversight on your part.

Second, filing doesn’t produce one by itself. Under the current Form 706 instructions, the IRS issues a closing letter only when someone requests it through Pay.gov and pays the user fee in effect at the time. Those instructions also tell requesters to wait at least nine months after filing before asking. And the IRS points executors to an account transcript as a no-charge alternative showing the same account activity. If a beneficiary wants documentation, those are the two roads, and the transcript is the faster and cheaper of them.

Your state might disagree with the IRS

Everything above is federal. It is not the whole story.

A number of states run their own estate tax, inheritance tax, or both — entirely separate from the federal system, and at thresholds that can sit far below the federal figure. Some tax the estate itself. A few tax the person who inherits instead, which is a different design with different rules about who owes what.

Which states do this, and at what dollar amount, changes over time. This book isn’t going to print a fixed list of states and numbers, because printing last year’s figure as this year’s fact is exactly the kind of mistake that gets someone an unpleasant letter from a state revenue department two years from now. Check your own state’s department of revenue directly — not a federal page, and not a search result that’s three years old — even when the federal Form 706 doesn’t apply to you at all. An estate with no federal filing obligation can still owe a state one, and a few states tax amounts the federal government would never look at twice.

Bev’s estate never came close to the federal threshold, and Ohio never asked her estate for a dime beyond what Chapter 8’s income tax returns already covered. That isn’t a promise about your state. It’s a reason to spend the ten minutes checking rather than assuming your state works the way Ohio happened to.

The threshold test

Here’s the tool for this chapter, and it’s short on purpose.

  1. Add up everything the person owned, valued as of the date of death: real estate, accounts, investments, business interests, vehicles, and anything else of value.
  2. Add any life-insurance proceeds and trust interests a lawyer or CPA tells you count toward the gross estate under the current Form 706 instructions.
  3. On its own line, add adjusted taxable gifts — lifetime gifts that have to come back into this calculation — and any specific exemption. If you don’t know whether gifts were made, that line is a question for a professional, not a zero.
  4. Write the date of death next to the total, and write next to it which year’s federal threshold applies — $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths, $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths. Compare the total from lines 1 through 3, not line 1 alone.
  5. If that total is nowhere close to the threshold, and no portability election is being made for a surviving spouse, check your state’s department of revenue for its own estate or inheritance tax, and otherwise set this chapter aside.
  6. Call an estate-tax professional this week, not next month, if any of these are true. The total is anywhere close to the federal number. There’s a business, farm or out-of-state real estate in the mix. A prior taxable gift was ever made, or you can’t rule one out. Or there’s a surviving spouse and nobody has filed anything yet.

Six lines. If your answer lands on line five, you’re done with the chapter in about the time Sam took with Bev’s numbers.

When this is not a do-it-yourself afternoon

A business interest. Farmland. Real estate in a second state. A gift made years ago that might count against the lifetime exemption. An estate sitting anywhere near the threshold once life insurance and trust interests are added in. A surviving spouse, with nothing filed yet, and a due date that may already be close.

Any one of those is a reason to hire an estate-tax professional, not a reason to keep reading chapters and hoping the arithmetic works out in your favor. This is the one part of the job where guessing wrong doesn’t just cost you an afternoon at the courthouse. It costs money, and sometimes it costs an election that can’t be taken back once its own window closes.

Gifts made while they were alive

One more wrinkle belongs in this chapter: lifetime gifts. A person can generally give a certain amount to any one recipient each year without it counting against their lifetime exemption. The IRS calls that the annual exclusion, and the figure changes periodically, so check the current year’s number rather than one remembered from somewhere else. Gifts above that yearly amount generally get reported on the giver’s own gift tax return and reduce the exemption available later.

What that means for you as executor is the adjusted-taxable-gifts line from the opening section. If the person made large gifts in their lifetime — helping a grandchild buy a house, say, or transferring a chunk of a business — those gifts can come back into the Form 706 calculation. The money is long gone. The exemption it used isn’t.

You likely won’t know whether this happened from the estate’s current paperwork alone. So ask whoever did their taxes, and ask directly: did they ever file a gift tax return? If the answer is yes, or even “I’m not sure,” that’s a question for the estate-tax professional, not a guess made from old bank statements.

Why this chapter stays short on purpose

I asked Sam once why he didn’t just hand me a flowchart for all of this instead of talking me through it over his desk. He said a flowchart works fine right up until somebody’s situation doesn’t fit one of its boxes. Estate tax is full of situations that don’t fit the boxes — a business interest here, an old gift there, a spouse who remarried. A ten-minute conversation catches the thing a chart would have missed.

That’s the spirit of this chapter. It isn’t trying to turn you into someone who can fill out a Form 706. It’s trying to get you to the six-line test fast, tell you honestly when the answer is “you’re fine,” and tell you just as honestly when the answer is “stop reading and make the call.” For Bev, it was the first answer, at a desk above an insurance agency in Chillicothe. If it’s the second answer for you, make the call this week — before the nine months run.

So add up the three lines. Then put the folder down, or pick up the phone.

Chapter 10: Handing It Out Without Blowing Up the Family

Kevin called me about the pickup eleven days after we buried our father.

He was in Tucson. He’d flown home for the funeral and flown back, and the truck was sitting in Dad’s driveway in Ohio with a dead battery and four inches of leaves on the hood. Dad had told him twice, over the years, that the pickup was his. I believed Kevin. I still believe him. The will didn’t mention it, the inventory hadn’t been filed, and I’d been the personal representative for less than two weeks.

What I wanted to say was yes. He’s my brother and he’d just lost his father too.

What I did instead was ask for a day.

Why the order matters more than the fairness

The job has a sequence, and the sequence is the whole reason an executor can be held responsible for money that is no longer in the estate.

Claims come first. Then you hold back enough to cover taxes and the costs of administration. Only then does distribution happen, with whatever authority your state’s process requires. Partial distributions, where they’re allowed, need authority behind them, a reserve big enough to cover what’s still outstanding, and written advice from the estate’s lawyer any time you can’t say for certain what the estate still owes. Your state’s rules and any order the court has entered are what actually control this, not the order I’m giving you.

Notice what that means in practice. Every dollar you hand over early is a dollar you may have to find again. If a late claim arrives after you’ve emptied the account, the people holding the money are your relatives, and the person who has to get it back from them is you. If you can’t get it back, the question becomes whether you should have paid it out in the first place. Chapter 7’s claim triage sheet exists so that question never gets asked about your estate.

That’s the arithmetic that answered Kevin. Not whether he deserved the truck. Whether I could prove, on the day I handed him the keys, that the estate didn’t need what the truck was worth.

The mistake that has a name on it

Early distribution is an executor’s error, and it doesn’t feel like an error while you’re making it. It feels like kindness. Somebody is grieving, somebody needs the money, somebody has waited long enough, and the estate has a balance sitting in it that’s clearly going to them eventually.

The word doing the work in that sentence is “clearly.”

You don’t know what the estate owes until your state’s claim period has run and you’ve worked through what came in. You don’t know what the final tax picture looks like until the returns from Chapter 8 are filed and whatever was due has been paid. Until both of those are true, the number you think is the residue is an estimate wearing a disguise.

The Federal Trade Commission, in its guidance on the debts of people who have died, lists being legally responsible for settling an estate and failing to follow your state’s probate laws among the situations in which a family member can end up personally responsible for a debt. Distributing before the law said you could is one way to walk into that. Not the only way. A common one.

So the default answer to “can I have it now” is “not yet, and here’s when I’ll know.” That is a different sentence from “no.” It has a date in it.

What your state may let you do sooner

Some payments and partial distributions can happen before the end of the case, and this is where I have to stop being useful in a general way. Whether you may pay funeral costs, an allowance to a surviving spouse or minor child, the costs of administration, a secured debt or an expense that keeps property from falling apart depends entirely on where the estate is being administered. Some states permit it. Some require it. Some put conditions on the amount or require a court’s blessing first.

There’s no national rule here, and a book that prints one is guessing with your money.

Ask two different people two different questions. The probate clerk can tell you which form a request like that uses in your court and when it has to be filed. The estate’s lawyer tells you whether you have the authority to make the payment at all, and from which funds. That split is the same one Chapter 4 set out, and it matters more here than anywhere, because this is the chapter where money actually leaves.

Write down whichever answer you get. Date it, and note who told you. If a beneficiary later asks why the house payment got made in March and their check didn’t come until November, that line is your answer.

Nobody receives anything without signing for it

When you do distribute, every item and every dollar leaves against a signature.

A receipt-and-release is the ordinary instrument for this: the person receiving acknowledges in writing what they got, that it’s their share, and that they’re releasing you with respect to it. The form, the wording and what it does legally vary by state, and the estate’s lawyer should draft or review yours. I’m not going to print a template for a document whose effect depends on fifty different bodies of law.

What I will tell you is why it earns its keep beyond the obvious.

Chapter 11 explains the closing paperwork your state may require. The warning belongs here. A release signed by someone who feels they were kept in the dark is a release you may end up defending. So let the lawyer draft the wording, and make sure nobody is seeing the estate’s numbers for the first time on the day you hand them a pen.

The cooperation of the people waiting on you is worth something to your sanity, and in some states it’s worth something concrete at the end. You don’t get that cooperation by appearing in November with a stack of paper and a pen. You get it by keeping people informed from February onward, so that by the time you ask for a signature, nobody feels like they’re signing something they haven’t been allowed to see.

The item that isn’t there anymore

Wills name specific things. Estates don’t always still have them.

A will drafted in 2004 may leave a named grandchild a car sold in 2019, a savings account closed when the bank merged, or a house that was refinanced and then sold to pay for care. What happens to that gift is a question of state law and of how the will itself is worded, and it isn’t a question you should settle at the kitchen table with the person who was supposed to receive it. Take the will’s exact words and the evidence of what happened to the item to the estate’s lawyer, and get the answer in writing before you tell anyone anything.

Then tell them yourself, early, rather than letting them discover it when the distributions go out. A person who learns in month three that the item is gone has a disappointment. A person who learns in month eleven, on the day everyone else gets their share, has a grievance.

The part that causes more fights than money

Personal property is where estates go sideways. Not the brokerage account. The dining room set, the tools, the photographs, the ring that three people remember being promised.

Money divides cleanly. A quilt doesn’t.

Four approaches have worked for people I know, and all four work better than the alternative, which is letting items leave the house one carload at a time while nobody keeps a list.

The round-robin pick. Draw an order, then take turns choosing one item each, round after round, until everyone passes. The person who picks last in round one picks first in round two.

The sealed bid. Everyone writes down what they’d pay for a contested item, in an envelope, same day. High bid takes it and the amount comes off their share. This one needs the lawyer’s sign-off, because you’re selling estate property to a beneficiary, and that’s precisely the transaction a fiduciary has to be careful about.

The three-things letter. Before anyone comes to the house, ask every person in writing to name the three things they most want and why. Most lists overlap less than families expect. The ones that do overlap are now identified before anybody is standing in a bedroom.

And the rule I’d keep even if I dropped the other three: the house gets emptied once, together, on a day everyone can attend. One day. Everyone there, or everyone represented by someone they chose. Nobody gets a private afternoon with the place.

Whatever method you use, write down what went where. Item, person, date, signature. That list is part of the same record the court or your state’s process will eventually ask you to account for.

The monthly update

Of every tool in this book, this is the one I’d argue hardest for.

Every month, on the same date, send every person entitled to a share the same short written update. Whether or not anything happened. Whether or not they’ve asked. Six lines:

  1. What came into the estate this month, in one sentence each.
  2. What went out, and to whom, in one sentence each.
  3. What I’m waiting on, and from whom.
  4. What I expect to happen next.
  5. When the next update goes out.
  6. What I need from you, if anything.

For Aunt Bev’s estate I sent eleven of these over fourteen months. Email to the people who read email, a one-page letter to the one who didn’t. Some months line three was the only line with anything in it. I sent it anyway. That’s my own habit rather than any state’s requirement, and your court may require a formal accounting on its own schedule regardless of what you send out informally.

Two things happened because of those eleven pages. Nobody ever had to ask me what was going on, which saved me the phone calls. And when I finally needed signatures, I was asking people who already knew every number I was about to show them.

The update took me about fifteen minutes. It saved more phone calls than I could count.

When to stop and get your own lawyer

There’s a line in this job, and I want you to recognize it from the far side.

If someone challenges the will. If a beneficiary demands a formal accounting. If anyone says the word “sue,” or stops talking to you and starts talking to a lawyer of their own. If you’re asked to do something you think is wrong and the person asking has a share of the estate.

Stop distributing. Stop deciding. Get a lawyer for the estate, and ask whether the circumstances mean you also need one for yourself, because those are not always the same lawyer and the difference matters when somebody is accusing you personally.

Where the court allows it, the estate’s legal fees come out of the estate. Sam put it to me plainly during Bev’s case: an hour of his time, asked at the start of a problem, cost a fraction of what the same problem costs after it’s been handled wrong for three months. He billed in six-minute increments and he was still the cheapest part of that year.

Don’t try to be even-handed and your own counsel at the same time. Those two jobs pull in different directions.

How to say no in writing

Which brings me back to Kevin and the truck.

I called him the next evening and told him no, and then I sent an email, because a phone call isn’t a record and because I wanted him to be able to read it twice without me in his ear. Four sentences, and I’ve used the same four shapes for every version of this conversation since.

Sentence one: what you asked me for, stated accurately and without hedging it.

Sentence two: the answer, which in this case was that I couldn’t release the pickup yet.

Sentence three: the reason, in plain words, with the stage of the process named. The inventory hadn’t been filed, the estate’s debts weren’t yet known, and I didn’t have the authority to hand over property that might be needed to pay them.

Sentence four: what happens next, with a date. I’d know more after the inventory was filed, I’d tell him what I learned, and the truck wasn’t going anywhere in the meantime.

That’s the whole letter. No apology for doing the job. No explanation of fiduciary duty. No sentence beginning “I know this is hard,” which is true and helps nobody.

What I’d add now, having done this twice more since: say in writing that you’re saying no to the timing, not to the person, when that’s actually what’s happening. Kevin wasn’t wrong about what Dad had said. He was early.

What it cost, and what it saved

Kevin was angry for about six weeks. He told a cousin I was being rigid. He was polite with me on the phone in a way that was worse than if he’d shouted.

He got the pickup. It took most of a year, and I pulled the battery and kept it on a trickle charger in our garage through the winter so the thing would start when the day came. When the estate could release it, I had the paperwork ready and he had the truck inside a week.

Here’s the part I didn’t expect. Three years later, when our mother died and I was doing it again, Kevin was the one who told the rest of the family to leave me alone and let the process run. He’d watched it work once. He remembered that the answer had a date in it and that the date had been true.

Say no to the timing. Then keep the date you gave.

Chapter 11: Closing the File, Getting Paid, and Getting Out Clean

Fourteen months after Bev died, I parked outside the Ross County courthouse for what I was fairly sure would be the last time.

I’d been there enough that the deputy clerk at the Letters window knew my face. This time I wasn’t at that window. I was in a courtroom with a folder an inch and a half thick, waiting for a judge to sign one piece of paper that would end a job I’d started at Bev’s kitchen table with a legal pad and no idea what “letters testamentary” meant.

The hearing took eleven minutes. The drive home took longer, and I spent most of it trying to name the feeling. It wasn’t relief exactly. It was closer to what you feel setting down a box you’ve carried so long your arms don’t trust that it’s gone.

The last accounting
