Before anyone signs anything, you account for every dollar, from the first day to the last.

This is where Chapter 4’s logbook and Chapter 5’s money notebook finally pay for themselves. Every dollar that came in — the accounts you consolidated, anything you sold, interest the estate account earned. Every dollar that went out — debts paid once Chapter 7’s claim period ran, taxes paid once Chapter 8’s and Chapter 9’s returns were settled, your own reimbursements, the lawyer’s fees. If you kept the log the way Ruth from month one told you to, this accounting is mostly transcription. If you didn’t, this is the month you find out what that cost you.

Your state may require the final account or a notice of the proposed closing to be served on people entitled to a share. Follow the court’s written instructions and the estate lawyer’s direction on who receives what, and when. In California, the state courts’ probate self-help pages say the final account doesn’t have to be filed if everyone entitled to distribution signs a written waiver of account or a written acknowledgment of receipt of their share. Skipping the account does not erase the final report, petition for final distribution, notice, or court decision that California still requires. Ask your estate lawyer what your state permits. I’d sent eleven monthly updates for exactly this reason. By the time I needed signatures, nobody was reading anything for the first time.

The petition, the hearing, and the piece of paper that ends it

What you file next has a different name in every state, but the first steps rhyme: ask the court to approve what you did and approve what’s left to distribute.

In California, the final report, account when required, and petition for final distribution come first. The judge reviews the accounting, confirms the distribution plan, and signs an order. After the court’s distribution order has been carried out, a personal representative may use Form DE-295 to ask for a final discharge — a separate, later step, not something that happens at the same hearing.

Your state may use another sequence or name, so have the estate lawyer identify the document that ends your appointment before you close the account. Ask the clerk what yours is called and get it well before you expect to need it, because an estate rarely closes exactly on schedule.

Can you get paid for this

Yes, in most states, and the honest answer about how much is unsatisfying: it depends entirely on where you are.

Some states set executor compensation as a statutory percentage of the estate. Others use a “reasonable compensation” standard that a court has to approve. California falls into the first group, and its self-help guide notes that representative and attorney fees there are set by law as a percentage and usually aren’t paid until the end of the case. There’s no national average I can hand you, because there isn’t one — not one that’s verifiable, and a book that printed one would be guessing with your money the same way Chapter 7 wouldn’t guess with your creditors.

Ask the clerk which form and filing date your court uses for compensation. Ask the estate’s lawyer what your state’s rule allows, whether approval is required, and when you may take a fee. Write the answer down with the date, the same as every other answer in this book.

The tax trap hiding in your own paycheck

Here’s the part that catches people who didn’t see it coming.

A fee you take for serving as executor is taxable income to you. An inheritance, generally, is not. If you’re both the executor and a beneficiary — which describes most readers of this book — that difference is arithmetic worth doing before you decide what to take, not after.

Sometimes waiving the fee and taking your share as an inheritance instead comes out ahead once you account for the tax. Sometimes it doesn’t, especially if the estate is large enough that every dollar matters to beneficiaries other than you. This is a CPA question, not an internet one, and it’s worth one more call to whoever did the estate’s income tax returns in Chapter 8 before you file anything that sets your compensation in stone.

What you are liable for, said plainly

You are not personally responsible for the debts your parent or aunt left behind simply because you’re related to them. That was true in Chapter 7 and it’s still true now.

What can make you personally liable is handling the job wrong. The Federal Trade Commission’s guidance on this lists it as one of a short set of exceptions: a person legally responsible for settling an estate who didn’t follow state probate law can end up owing the money themselves. Distributing before the claim period ran, as Chapter 10 warned against. Paying the wrong creditor ahead of one with a stronger legal claim. Commingling estate money with your own, which Chapter 5 told you never to do for exactly this reason.

None of those are things that happen to you. They’re things you do, usually in a hurry, usually meaning well. The whole point of every log, every letter, every written answer this book has asked you to keep is that if anyone ever questions a decision you made, you can show your reasoning and the date you made it. That record is your protection, and it’s the cheapest insurance you’ll ever carry.

Two federal tax forms to discuss with the CPA

Two IRS forms are worth raising with the CPA before you consider the estate closed on the tax side.

Form 4810 requests prompt assessment of certain income-tax returns; it does not itself discharge you. Form 5495, filed after the relevant returns, requests discharge from personal liability for the decedent’s income, gift, and estate taxes. Neither form replaces state-court closing steps, creditor rules, or advice on this estate. Read the current instructions for each one — these aren’t forms to fill out from memory of what a book told you in 2026.

What to keep, and for how long

There’s no single answer here either, and I’d rather tell you that plainly than invent a number that sounds tidier than it is.

The IRS ties how long you keep a record to how long that record’s return could still be questioned. Generally three years. Six years if income was underreported by more than a quarter of what was shown. Seven years for a claim involving worthless securities or a bad debt. Indefinitely if a return was never filed at all. And separately, for anything that shows what a piece of property was worth, keep that record until the limitation period runs out for the year the property is eventually sold — because whoever inherited it will need that number for their own taxes someday, not just you for yours.

Your state’s probate rules or the estate’s lawyer may ask for longer than the IRS does. Take whichever date is latest.

My own habit — and I want to be clear this is habit, not rule — was one labeled banker’s box, kept seven years, with a sticky note on the lid listing what was inside and when it could go. It’s not a number anyone has to follow. It’s just long enough that I stopped worrying about it, which was worth something to me even if it isn’t required of you.

Closing the account, closing the EIN, closing the file

The last few administrative items, in the order I did them for Bev.

Close the estate bank account once every check has cleared and every return is filed. Mark the estate’s final income tax return as final, exactly as the instructions say to. File any outstanding returns and pay whatever’s due — nothing closes cleanly with an unfiled return sitting behind it. The EIN itself can’t be canceled; it’s the estate’s permanent federal number for as long as the estate existed. What you can do is ask the IRS to deactivate the account once everything’s filed and paid, following whatever its current written procedure asks for. And file Form 56 one more time — not to start the fiduciary relationship this time, but to tell the IRS it’s over.

Each of those is a small task. Together they’re the difference between a file that’s actually closed and one that looks closed until a letter arrives eighteen months from now addressed to an estate nobody’s watching anymore.

When something arrives after the door is shut

It will happen to someone reading this. A dividend check for forty dollars. A refund nobody expected. A bill from a hospital that took its time.

If the estate account is already closed and the discharge order is already signed, don’t assume you can simply handle it yourself the way you might have in month three. Call the lawyer who handled the closing and ask what your state’s process is for a late asset or a late claim against an estate that’s already been distributed. Some states have a simple mechanism for exactly this. Others want the file reopened. Either way, it’s a phone call, not a decision you make alone at your own kitchen table.

The drive home

I didn’t cry at the hearing. I’d expected to, and I didn’t.

What got me was turning onto the county road toward the house, the same road I’d driven to Sam’s office that first Thursday fourteen months earlier, legal pad still in the car, not yet knowing what any of the forms were called. I knew all of them now. That was the whole difference between that drive and this one.

Dale had supper waiting, and he didn’t ask how it went until I’d sat down. “Signed,” I told him. He nodded like that settled something for him too, and it probably did — he’d made his own supper more nights that year than either of us had counted.

The tool: the closing checklist, and the keep-until rule

Fifteen items, roughly in the order they come due. Check each against your state court’s current instructions and your county probate clerk before treating any of them as finished.

  1. Final accounting complete: every dollar in, every dollar out, since day one.
  2. If your state allows it, the signed paperwork gathered that lets the final account be skipped.
  3. Petition for final distribution (or your state’s equivalent) filed.
  4. Hearing date confirmed; attend in case the judge has questions.
  5. Discharge order (or your state’s equivalent) received — the actual piece of paper, not just a verbal “you’re done.”
  6. Executor compensation: confirm the court’s form and filing date with the clerk, legal entitlement and required approval with the estate’s lawyer, and tax treatment with the CPA before taking any fee.
  7. Form 4810 considered with the CPA, if prompt assessment is something you want.
  8. Form 5495 considered with the CPA, once the relevant returns are filed.
  9. Final income tax return marked final, exactly as its instructions direct.
  10. All outstanding returns filed, all tax due paid.
  11. EIN deactivation requested once every return is filed and every tax is paid.
  12. Form 56 filed again, to tell the IRS the fiduciary relationship has ended.
  13. Estate bank account closed, only after every check has cleared.
  14. Distribution records and receipts copied to beneficiaries who’ll need basis information for inherited property.
  15. Records boxed, labeled, and dated for disposal using the keep-until rule below.

The keep-until rule, one line per record. First: which return does this support, and when does that return’s limitation period end. Second: does it show the basis of property a beneficiary still owns — if so, keep it and give that beneficiary a copy. Third: did the discharge order, the court, or the estate’s lawyer set a longer period than the tax rules require. Take whichever date is latest, write it on the box, and don’t open the box again until that date arrives.

What You’ll Know in a Year

Jess called on a Sunday, almost exactly a year after the discharge order came through, to ask something she’d clearly been sitting on. Her father-in-law was sick, and he had named her somewhere in his will, probably as a backup.

“If it’s actually me,” she said, “what’s the one thing you’d tell me before I said yes?”

I was at the sink, and I didn’t answer right away, because I wanted to give her something true instead of something that sounded good on the phone.

I told her to write things down, ask before guessing, and let the required order outrank her instinct.

You don’t need a law degree for any of that. You need a notebook, a habit of checking the court’s written instructions for forms and deadlines, and enough stubbornness to say “I don’t know yet; I’ll ask the estate lawyer” when the question is about authority, liability, or a disputed decision.

Then she asked the question underneath the first one. Could she say no, and would saying it make her the kind of person who says no.

You can decline before appointment because you lack the time or can’t be even-handed. Tell the alternate and check with the court what to file. After appointment, don’t simply walk away; ask the estate lawyer how to step down under your state’s rules. A no before you’re appointed is a scheduling fact and a fairness fact. A no after you’re appointed is a legal step with a procedure attached, which is a different animal and not one to improvise.

What the job gives you back isn’t peace about the death. Nothing I did for Bev made losing her hurt less. What it gave me was something smaller and, it turns out, more useful: at the end of fourteen months, I could account for every dollar and every decision, out loud, to anyone who asked. Kevin asked, eventually, mostly out of curiosity by then. I had an answer for every line. That’s not closure. That’s just not having anything to be afraid of when the phone rings.

She wanted to know which single piece of paper she should hang onto if she kept nothing else. If a court appoints you, keep the Letters or order and ask each institution whether it needs a certified copy. A small-estate affidavit is different: check your state’s conditions and the institution’s requirements before using it; it does not give you general executor authority. Ask an estate lawyer if your powers are unclear. I have watched people assume one document opens every door, and then stand at a teller window learning otherwise with a line behind them.

Here’s the part nobody warned me about, and I’d want somebody to warn her.

The year is not dramatic. It’s boring. Two hard weeks at the front, two hard weeks at the end, and in between eleven months of waiting on other people’s calendars — a processing window, a claim period, a return that can’t go anywhere until a form arrives in February. For me, waiting was the hardest part to stay dutiful inside of. The weeks I nearly let things slide weren’t the sad weeks. They were the flat ones, when the folder sat on the dining room table with no reason to open it, so I stopped opening it. Then I’d lost a week of the notebook and had to rebuild it out of memory. That’s the one thing I’ve spent this whole book telling you not to do.

Jess asked whether it cost me anything. Yes, and not money, because the estate paid me back. Saturdays, mostly. If you’re married, say the sentence out loud before you say yes to the court: this is going to eat our weekends for about a year. Let the other person be annoyed in advance instead of ambushed in month four.

Then she asked something nobody had asked me. Did I ever get angry at Bev.

I put the dish down for that one.

Twice that I remember clearly, and both times over paperwork she could have left in better shape and didn’t. Not because she was careless — because she thought there was time. Being angry at somebody who can’t answer you is a thin, strange feeling, and it passes, and it doesn’t mean you loved her less. It means you were tired and the file was short a page. If it happens to Jess, I told her, notice it, let it be true for an afternoon, and don’t say it to the family. They’re not in the file. They’ll hear it as something it isn’t.

I told Jess the map is short enough to say in one breath, so she’d remember it standing in a kitchen the way I was. Decide. Appoint. Find. Open. Pay. File. Distribute. Close. The map helps me remember the work; your state’s procedure, any court order and tax deadlines set the actual sequence. Ask the estate lawyer when steps collide.

She asked what happens if she’s named executor before her father-in-law has even had the conversation about a will. That’s a different book — Estate Planning for Beginners — and I told her so, by title. The questions about writing a will, naming beneficiaries and setting up a power of attorney live there, not here. And if her mother-in-law is the one who dies first and Jess needs help with arrangements, mail, and the first weeks before appointment, that’s The First 90 Days After a Parent Dies. This book starts when someone is deciding whether to serve or has been appointed.

One more thing, and I saved it for last on purpose. Your state court’s self-help site and your county probate clerk have the current forms and deadlines; nothing in this book replaces them. For a question with real weight behind it — your authority, your exposure, a rule two people read two different ways — that belongs to a lawyer who knows your state, not a guess from a book written three years before you needed it. I wasn’t guessing when I told Bev’s estate’s lawyer I didn’t understand something. I asked. Every time. That’s the only part of this I’d insist on if I could insist on just one.

Jess was quiet for a second, then said she’d call Dale next, since he’d lived through the whole thing standing next to me and might remember parts I didn’t.

“He’ll tell you about the thermos,” I said. “Ask him anyway.”

She laughed, and we talked about something else for a while. That was the end of it. Not a lesson. Just a phone call between two people — one who now knew what “letters testamentary” meant, and one who didn’t yet, and might never need to.
